Drones are even used to retrieve weapons from the battlefield. Here you can see “Hornet Queen” picking weapons on the battlefield using a magnet. In December 2023, Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy set the task of producing a million drones for the Ukrainian Armed Forces. By now, the task has been completed, says Ukraine’s minister of digital transformation Mykhailo Fedorov. There are already contracts for the production of a million of drones for the Ukrainian army. They include standard FPV drones, long-range, reconnaissance and other types of drones that are already used by the Ukrainian defenders at the front. Just imagine this number: 1,000,000 drones! It’s 2 drones per each Russian soldier on the Ukrainian land. But tens of thousands of drones go directly from manufacturers to the Ukrainian units at the front without involving the government and the ministry of defense. They are paid for from donations that people make on behalf of certain units. So, if a certain unit requires more drones, they place a request with a manufacturer they know, and get a delivery within days, without the need for ministerial approvals. This is why the Ukrainian army is so much more efficient, and why the Russian soldiers say that it feels like the Ukrainians have 50:1 advantage in drones. This also saves thousands of Ukrainian lives.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What will happen if Russia runs out of manpower for the military?
Answer: August 2024: Russian soldiers surrender en masse in the Kursk region of Russia, overpowered and outnumbered by the Ukrainian forces in their own territory. How the tables have turned: The photos of the annihilated Russian column that was bringing soldiers to the front in the Kursk region are all over the Russian social networks. The Russian correspondents first showed the column moving through the Kursk region, and then other Russians filmed it burning and the aftermath of the attack. The FSB arrested a man who filmed the burning trucks and made him confess that he was doing it on orders of the Ukrainians. Someone has to be blamed for the major security screw up! And another Russian propagandist from the military channel ‘Zvezda’ (‘Star’) was proudly filming another Russian column going through the Kursk region yesterday — already after the previous column got burned. Learning from their mistakes is for the wimps. Russian propaganda professionals are trained in bragging and boasting, not tactical stealth. There are basically no professionally trained junior army officers with combat experience left in Russia — almost all of them are dead by now. That’s why the screwups like the one with the burned column become possible — no one learned the instructions clearly stating that when resting, soldiers need to spread and hide, as opposed to stopping on the side of the road with no gaps between the vehicles, with the personnel remaining in the trucks. It looks more likely with every day that Russia will have to do another mass mobilization, to compensate for the terrible losses at the front. In order to achieve the "goals of the SMO" as Putin formulated them, the Russian army would need to call up another 3-4 million men — at least 1.5 million of them would end up killed or maimed, until it becomes obvious to everyone in Russia that achieving Putin’s stated goals is simply impossible. Despite Kremlin’s constantly raising payouts for signing up to go to the war, the number of Russian “volunteers” has dropped sharply — there are (almost) no fools left to die for money — even rather large sums of money (by the Russian standards). By 2024, Ukraine has more soldiers to fight off Russia than Russia has “contractors” who agreed to go to another country and become murderers, in hopes to pay off their debts. The Russian propagandists promote the idea that the Ukrainian army will run out of people faster because the Ukrainian population is smaller. It is true, the Ukrainian population is smaller — but that’s not all the truth: the attacking army needs to have a multifold numerical advantage to succeed. But the Russian army has no such advantage. On top of that, Russia is undoubtedly behind the Ukrainian army in technological terms. Even if Russia could manage to mobilize and equip 3–4 million soldiers, they still wouldn’t be able to close the technological gap. When Russia attacked Ukraine in February 2022, they had an enormous advantage in terms of manpower and weapons — but the balance has been slowly shifting to the other side. By now, Ukraine has the advantage of the modern technology and weapons, as well as the backing of the economies producing over 50% of the global GDP. Putin is not only running out of manpower, but also out of stockpiles of the Soviet weapons and money to finance the military production and the army. The Ukrainian incursion in the Kursk region further destabilizes the whole system. Putin has no time to mobilize the manpower. It’s not impossible that the whole Russian front in Ukraine might collapse. Follow me for more updates!

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How do Russian pilots drop glide bombs?
Answer: Russian military correspondents confirmed that the Russian pilots are dropping glide bombs on Russian towns in the Kursk region, which are under control of the Ukrainian armed forces. According to Z-correspondents, “the order has been confirmed at the very top.” The same pilots who bombed with glide bombs Ukrainian Bakhmut and Vovchansk are now bombing the Russian towns near the border, on orders of the Russian generals. The population of the territories under control of the Ukrainian Armed Forces and their property have been already written off by Putin. Putin ordered to pay each refugee 10,000 ruble (USD $115). Generous offer in the usual Putin’s style. To get this generous payout, one only needs to gather proper documentation on the lost property: compile an inventory, confirm the losses with documents, and get an official valuation. Just over 10 certificates — and to get some of these papers, one has to pay a fee. And only those whose registered place of residence was destroyed, only they can get $115 — and only for 1 property, not for all the houses they might own. That is, you are a refugee, you had to escape in a hurry, leaving everything behind — and the officials demand that you confirm that you are from there and owned the property that you lost, for $100 of Putin's aid. No doubt, the local and Moscow officials will steal most of the allocated funds. It’s Russia, after all.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: If Ukraine conducts virtual referendums in Russian-controlled Krasnodar, Stavropol, Rostov-on-Dov, Belgorod, Voronezh, and Kursk, and if >100% of participants vote to leave Russia and to join Ukraine, then which countries will recognize the results?

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What exactly does Ukraine hope to achieve by launching an incursion into Russian territory?
Answer: TAP ON THE PHOTO TO VIEW. A column of Russian troops was obliterated in the Kursk region. 12 trucks with infantry were on the way to fight the Ukrainian incursion. 100 Russian soldiers killed. (Video in the comments below.) For 2.5 years of the war, the Russian propaganda was pumping threats of “unimaginable response” if Russia were to lose. Portraying Putin as “insane” and ready to start dropping nukes at any second. And it worked. European officials were terrified of angering Putin, they wanted to "save his face." Russian “liberal opposition” echoed them, calling Putin and Medvedev crazy, warning that they are capable of unthinkable. The Kursk incursion showed it was only a bluff. The Ukrainian Forces crossed the border into Russia — and they aren’t leaving. So, what is the Russian government doing? The same Russians who threatened the world with nukes when a western politician simply said something, the same Russians are trying to pretend that nothing is happening when foreign troops actually invaded Russia. Putin’s gangsters are prepared to do anything to maintain the illusion of a quiet life for Russians. That’s the main takeaway of this whole operation in the Kursk region.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What kind of drone might have been used in the attack on a Russian air base?
Answer: There is rarely a day without a Ukrainian drone attack on an airbase, a fuel depot, or an oil processing plant deep in the Russian territory. At first, Russians suspected that it were Ukrainian saboteurs that were launching drones near the strategic targets in Russia, but by now we know that Ukrainian drones can indeed fly that far into Russia. Last night, the Russians tried to transfer troops to Kursk via the Lipetsk military airfield. But things didn’t work as planned: the airfield was hit in a massive drone attack, with explosions and fires heard until the morning. Residents of Lipetsk posted videos of low-flying drones. The Lipetsk airfield is 285km from the front line. Videos show secondary detonations. Reportedly, the hits targeted ammunition storages where more than 700 guided bombs were stored. The airfield in Lipetsk housed several dozen fighter jets and helicopters. Most of them didn’t escape. The governor of the region insisted that the fire was extinguished by the morning, but photos made by locals prove otherwise. Residents of 4 nearby villages had to be evacuated. All entertainment shows in the region have been cancelled. There were also massive drone attacks last night in the Belgorod and Kursk regions. In the Kursk region, the incursion by the Ukrainian forces is ongoing. One of the most famous long-range kamikaze drones in the Ukrainian Defense Forces is the "Lyutyi" (“Fierce”). This drone is actively used for long-distance strikes on military targets. There were also Ukrainian drones sighted in Voronezh, Bryansk and Oryol regions, as well as over the territory of the occupied Crimea. According to the Russian ministry of defence, “all drones had been shot down, no losses”. The war is now firmly into the Russian territory.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What is the most likely path for the Ukrainian Armed Forces into the Russian territory starting in the Kursk region? Why?
Answer: The most likely path for the Ukrainian armed forces into the Kursk region is where the Russian troops aren’t present — or where the commanders choose not to resist. There are basically no “contract troops” in the Kursk region, only the units made of regular draftees — 18–19-year-old boys serving the compulsory 1-year term. These troops have been abandoned for 4 days, without communication from their superiors, with no food or water. The commanders told them to “stay there”, but draftees aren’t supposed to be used in combat. 5-million ruble death payouts are reserved only for the troops that are located in “the area of SMO” — on occupied Ukrainian territories. The troops located in the Kursk region aren’t in the war zone and won’t be paid for getting wounded or killed. They are also not getting paid 200,000 rub. ($2,400) per month in wages. So, many Russian commanders choose to surrender with their “bunch of teens in uniforms” as opposed to trying to fight against the experienced, combat-hardened Ukrainian units. Reportedly, small groups of the Ukrainian forces moved as far as 45 km in depth at some directions, towards strategic targets. They avoid battles and move forward where it’s easier to get through. And the main group of Ukrainian forces is moving steadily with all the logistics after them, clearing the islands of resistance of scattered Russian units. Captured Russian soldiers. Apparently, over 300 Russian soldiers have already surrendered, creating a logistical problem for tie Ukrainians — transport is required to take them to the Ukrainian territory, but trucks and cars are needed to support the offensive. Commander of the Ukrainian Armed Forces Syrskyi posted this photo from “the area near the offensive operations”. The Ukrainian commanders have a plan — I’d say, they have several plans — and they are following the path that’s the most advantageous in the current situation. And no one, except them, knows what is the overall plan. Let’s wait and see.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What if the Kursk disaster in 2000 had prevented Putin from getting to power? How would Russia have looked today?
Answer: Vladimir Putin’s presidential term started with Kursk nuclear submarine disaster on 12 August 2000. The submarine sank in the Barents Sea and all 118 personnel on board perished. The crews of nearby ships, which all were taking part in a large-scale naval exercise, felt two explosions, but the generals did not start any search for the vessel for 6 hours. The explosion was so powerful, it was recorded by seismologists in Alaska. It took over 16 hours to locate the submarine (the emergency rescue buoy had been switched off). It was finally located on the ocean floor at a depth of 108 metres (354 ft). Newly inaugurated Putin was on holiday and refused to cut his vacation short, to deal with the crisis. After the explosions, 23 sailors remained alive on the submarine — they died waiting to be rescued. Putin was refusing to allow foreigners to be part of the rescue mission, and Russians were unable to do what was needed to be done. Desperate relatives were waiting for news about their men at the quayside, growing more and more despondent because of the inaction by the state officials and the Navy. All this time Russian officials lied about what was happening. “The communication with the crew has been established, they are getting hot food!” was telling the Navy spokesman. Blatant lies. Only on August 20 — 8 days after the catastrophe — the Norwegian vessel ‘Seaway Eagle’ was allowed to begin working on the recovery mission. Norwegian divers did in 24 hours what the Russians could not do in a week — they managed to open the submarine's emergency escape hatch. But it was too late. All survivors of the accident were already dead. When the Russian TV — which was still reporting freely at the time — done an investigative piece on the tragedy and showed the widows of the marines, Putin accused the program in ”hiring whores for $10” to discredit him: “You hire whores on purpose. You gave them 10 dollars each, specifically to discredit me,” Putin claimed. It was after the Kursk disaster that Putin began raider seizures of the independent media. This was 24 years ago. Today, the words “Kursk” and “Putin” are again in the news, but this time it’s the Kursk region of Russia — and the Ukrainian troops’ incursion into Russia. And once again, Putin is lying about it. But this no longer surprises anyone. ”Kursk” disaster didn’t cripple Putin’s grasp on power — but maybe, Kursk will?

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Is Ukrainian army liberating Kursk region in Russia from Putin's regime? Will Jack Sullivan (likely controlled by Russia) and Joe Biden try to stop the Ukrainians and order them to go back to Ukraine?
Answer: TAP ON THE PIC TO VIEW. On the second day of Ukrainians’ incursion into the Kursk region, Vladimir Putin recorded a televised speech in front of his minions. Looking at his papers, the greatest geopolitician of our times announced that there is an armed incursion into the Kursk region, by the Ukrainians! As usual, Putin whined that he was deceived, misled and hoodwinked, and then complained about Ukrainians “shooting indiscriminately”. Russia itself always deliberately targets residential buildings, maternity hospitals and kids’ cancer clinics — but Ukrainians, they are “shooting indiscriminately.” In just 1 day, Russia lost more territory than the Russian army managed to gain in the last 3 months. The Ukrainian forces managed to get 15–20 km into the Russian territory and capture 11 settlements. Residents of Kurchatov are getting phone calls telling them about the imminent seizure of the Kursk Nuclear Power Plant by the Ukrainians. The Russian officials are furious about it and warn locals it’s a “Ukrainian psy op” and there are no worries whatsoever — but the city administration evacuated, just in case. Russian TV propagandists and Z-channels are saying, "The Ukrainian Armed Forces invaded the territory of Russia", when commenting on the fights in the Kursk region. Russian TV propagandists and Z-channels know too well that Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhya, and Kherson regions of Ukraine are not the territory of Russia — despite any Putin’s claims and re-written Russian Constitution. Everybody knows. The goal of the special operation by the Ukrainian military could be the capture of the Sudzha gas metering station. It’s the only point through which Russian gas enters the Ukrainian pipeline and then gets piped through to European consumers. Previously, transit also passed through another station, "Sokhranovka". However, Ukraine stopped accepting fuel through it, because the gas metering station was located on the territory of the occupied Luhansk region. If the gas metering station in Sudzha becomes inoperable, it would create an enormous problem for Russia, because they simply cannot replace the western equipment — due to sanctions. Obviously, it’s all part of the genius plan that has been meticulously implemented by the greatest geostrategist of all times.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: When is Putin going to see sense and note that his conventional military forces can’t take Ukraine let alone a NATO member?
Answer: This question is 2 years and 4 months old: it was asked on April 16, 2022 — less than 2 months after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In over 2 years, Putin hasn’t figured out that his war is doomed — and keeps destroying Russia, its past, present and future. Russia has lost its reputation of a strong military power, lost hundreds of thousands of men on the battlefield (and millions to emigration), destabilized and cannibalized its economy, wasted enormous human and material resources, got pushed out of its most lucrative international markets, exhausted its already worn out and under-maintained infrastructure, with no ability to afford capital investment. In July 2024, Russia managed to gain more territory (red dots) — and lost 50,000 men doing that. The situation looks even more pointless for Russia if we look at the larger map. In fact, Russia still controls about the same percentage of the Ukrainian territory as in December 2022 — and much less than 2 years ago. Russia’s territorial gains of “800 square km” in 2024, which the Russian ministry of defence brags about, should be viewed to scale — Ukraine is 603,628 square km in size. 800 square km is 0.13%. To gain it, Russia has lost 200,000 men. 2.5 years after the start of the full-scale war, Russia is still unable to gain the full control of Donetsk region — the goal that Putin announced since day 1. 2.5 years!! At this rate, Russia will reach the borders of the Donetsk region in a few decades, having burned down its entire male population. With every month, Russia has to throw in more men than before — but the gains are getting smaller, not bigger. There are many reasons for that, including the quality of new recruits — it dropped substantially since the start of the war, as well as increased sophistication of the warfare — by now, drones became the leading defense tool for Ukraine, and Russia is unable to keep up the pace. The war that Putin refuses to stop is eating Russia from the inside like cancer. The Russian Federation wanted to absorb Ukraine, but in the process started eating itself. If Russia doesn’t lose any of its territories as the result of this war, I’ll be very surprised.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: If Russia succeeded in dissolving Ukraine would there be insurgency with enough support like the Taliban? Would Russian troops be trapped in cities? How long would it take Russia to turn Ukraine into a fully submissive Russian territory?

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What's the problem with the freed Russian dissidents? Why do so many see them as pro-Russian whereas they were imprisoned in Russia?
Answer: Freed Russian dissidents Kara-Murza, Pivovarov and Yashin scored a tsunami of outrage online after their first post-exchange press-conference, where they talked more about the plight of “ordinary Russians” than about Putin’s genocidal war in Ukraine. Gabrielius Landsbergis, Lithuanian minister of Foreign Affairs, explained the issue in plain terms: “I would like to address the recurring question of those “ordinary Russians” who “shouldn’t be sanctioned”. Ordinary Russia is sick. Healing will be a long and gruelling process which can only start when Russia, not just Putin, is defeated. Without a defeat in Ukraine, Russia will just keep spreading. So about those “unfair” sanctions against “ordinary Russians”... Well, anything which slows down Russia’s total war machine will have ordinary Lithuanians’ support. Whatever victory takes,” concluded Landsbergis. Voicing narratives echoing Putin’s demands to Ukraine to cease fire and negotiate — with such conviction, didn’t score much love for the new additions to the Russian opposition in exile among the pro-Ukraine crowd. Andrei Pivovarov, one of the political prisoners that Germany asked for in exchange for the killer Krasikov, stated in an interview: Following the disastrous press-conference and personal interviews of Yashin and Pivovarov, the freed oppositionists had to explain their position and state clearly that they had always been — and still are — against Putin’s war in Ukraine and want Russia to withdraw its troops. Ilia Yashin went online and spent 2 hours and 23 minutes explaining himself and saying he was “a friend of Ukraine”. He explained how he and his friends were victims of the war in Ukraine (which Yashin called “conflict”) and that he wasn’t an enemy of Ukraine and that he always loved Ukraine, and that Putin is a criminal. That he [Yashin] was imprisoned because he spoke against the war and spent 2 years in prison, and that “it was a huge trauma” for him. That he tried to talk his cell mate out of signing up to go to the “SMO” and he nearly succeeded, but then he was locked in a punishment cell and while he was away, the guy signed the army contract, and then he was killed in Ukraine within weeks — “torn into pieces”, so he had to be buried in a closed coffin — and how this experience traumatized him [Yashin] and he is still upset about it. How he lost his homeland because of this war and was sent to Germany with nothing except a toothbrush — “not even a pair of socks and jocks”. And now he can’t walk around in Moscow with his friends. And that even though there are people who are now sitting under Russian bombs in Ukraine, he also lost a lot. He’s now “an illegal immigrant” in Germany with no proper documents, and can’t even leave to visit Austria, for instance. I must add, I did watch the part of Yashin’s stream that I’ve summarized here, and it was insufferable. To say that I lost my faith in the Russian liberal opposition is to put it mildly. The only real Russian opposition are those who fight Putin’s army with weapons in their hands, saboteurs within Russia, or those who donate to the Ukrainian army. The rest of “the anti-Putin Russians” in exile are “pink ponies” — inept wannabes with no backbone.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Why is Putin not withdrawing his forces from Ukraine?
Answer: Russia is bombing New York — a town in Donetsk region. (Video in the comments below.) New York (Niu-York), population 10,000 before the war, is a well-fortified section of the front and the last point on the pre-2022 demarcation line. Before the full-scale invasion unleashed by Russia in February 2022, the demarkation line between the Russian and Ukrainian positions was right behind the town. From the positions of the Ukrainian army near Niu-York, one could see the outskirts of Gorlovka, which had been occupied since 2014 and is located 6 km from Niu-York. That’s how far Russia “moved” in 2.5 years in Donetsk region, which was Putin’s openly stated goal from the start! Russia is doing what it always does — destroys the town and turns it into ruins, sending meat waves of freshly delivered cannon fodder into attacks, trying to move forward 100 meters, 200 meters, 500 meters. No matter how incremental and meaningless are the gains, Putin’s propagandists tell their flock that “Russia is moving forward and therefore winning”. In Kherson, which is close to the front line on the Ukrainian side, Russians are attacking civilians in the streets: drones are waiting for people and dropping explosives on elders, teens. When an ambulance comes to help the injured, drones attack the ambulance. The same happens in Zaporizhzhia. Putin is killing and terrorizing Ukrainian civilians — the tactic that the Russian army was employing since the first days of the invasion. This is Vitaly Zubkov from the Vologda village of Bolshoy Dvor. He was born on May 25, 2006. Height 154 cm/5 feet. Military nickname: Ambal (“Big Guy”). When Zubkov turned 18 a couple of months ago, he signed the contract to join the Russian army and was assigned to the 245th tank assault regiment and sent to the war. In early July, Zubkov's sister began searching for her brother, because he disappeared and wasn’t contacting the family. She was posting the card with his details into the chats where relatives of missing Russian soldiers are trying to connect with someone who has some information. At the end of July, the family was told that the teen had been killed. Born under Putin, went to school under Putin, died under Putin. What a life. Meanwhile, Russian mobile networks began sending mass SMS to customers offering to sign an army contract with the immediate payout on signup of at least 800,000 ruble (USD $9,400). Putin needs at least 25,000 new recruits every month, to continue the pressure of meat wave attacks at the long front. He still has the money, but the numbers of desperate Russians willing to play the death lottery are dwindling, and recruitment of foreign fighters is too complicated and doesn’t bring enough mercenaries. Besides, countries like India and Nepal are getting upset that their citizens are getting killed in Ukraine. Much easier to promise “big money” to poverty-stricken Russians, who are hoping to get out of slums. Putin refuses to withdraw his forces from Ukraine because he hopes that he will terrorize the Ukrainians into submission. He needs to prove he is a “master strategist” and a great ruler who expanded the borders of the Russian Federation — demonstrating that a bully and a murderer can take what he wants and no one can stop him. For as long as Ukraine resists, Putin has no hope of keeping the territory he captured. He needs Ukraine to stop fighting.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Should we consider Vladimir Kara-Murza and the other dissidents released in the Russia-West prisoner swap as dangerous extremists as Moscow claims or wrongfully detained political prisoners?
Answer: Putin’s regime considers Vladimir Kara-Murza, Andrei Pivovarov and Ilia Yashin “dangerous extremists”, Russian opposition in exile views them as wrongfully detained political prisoners — and Ukrainians view them as Russian imperialists. The split between the Ukrainians and the mainstream Russian political opposition to Putin’s regime keeps widening. The first interviews by Ilia Yashin — whom some Russian commentators immediately announced “the potential new leader of the Russian opposition” — infuriated the Ukrainians. The freshly released Yashin announced his undying love for Russia, said he’d prefer to be in in Russia to being in safety in Germany, and that his first wish when he was told he was now a free man was to buy a ticket and fly back to Russia (yes, for real) — and then pronounced that the best option for Ukrainians would be to ask for a ceasefire and begin to negotiate with Putin, so that “people stop dying”. In short, the most respected Russian oppositionist immediately began making demands to Ukrainians along the lines of demands of Putin, Lavrov, Zakharova, Medvedev and Co. Yashin said that he had a chance to talk to the FSB officers who accompanied him on the way from prison to the exchange, and these lovely FSB officers were friendly enough to share details on their recent deployment in Kharkiv region, and how bad were the losses, and that these losses needed to be stopped immediately. Kara-Murza and Pivovarov dropped similar bombshells, demanding to stop sanctions against “regular Russians” and stating that it’s Putin’s war, and “regular Russians” should be given visas and other perks by Europe. Frankly, their press conference would appear more appropriate if it were held in Stockholm. Let's sum it up: And the Russians who were freed with such great effort by hundreds of people around the globe: What did the world expect? But instead, the released Russians demanded to “lift the sanctions.” Imagine if the anti-Nazi activist Dietrich Bonhoeffer, instead of creating a resistance movement against the Nazi regime and participating in the assassination attempt on Hitler, traveled around the countries of the anti-Hitler coalition and talked about the "unjust suffering of ordinary Germans" because of the actions of these countries. The behavior of the released Russian prisoners makes sense if you understand that they are trying to please Russians, not Ukrainians. But the bitter truth is that the Russian opposition also utterly fails to please Russians.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Why did Russia want Vadim Krasikov so badly to be part of the largest US-Russia prisoner swap?
Answer: Vadim Krasikov is linked to Vladimir Putin since 1990s when he was stealing hundreds of millions of dollars with St. Petersburg’s mayor Anatoly Sobchak — Krasikov was a bodyguard for them, and obviously a silent witness to many shady deals. Putin’s judo trainer Leonid Usvyaytsov was part of St. Petersburg’s organized crime since the city was called Leningrad. It was Usvyaytsov who got teenage Putin into the law faculty of Leningrad State University under the sports quota. Reportedly, it was also Usvyaytsov who told young Vladimir to apply to the KGB to be an informer, which Putin became already at the university. Putin held Usvyaytsov in high regard and in his earlier years as the president of Russia spoke about him with utmost respect. It was Usvyaytsov who trained Putin in the framework of “understandings” (“ponyatia”) of “the thief’s code” of ethics, used in Russian criminals gangs and prisons — and now also among the Russian enforcers. Later all mentions of Leonid Usvyaytsov disappeared from the official Putin’s biography. Usvyaytsov crafted his poetic eulogy while still alive, it’s on his memorial stone: “I died, but mafia is immortal”. So, when Putin became Sobchak’s curator from the KGB, he connected the city administration not only with the secret services but also with the organized crime, which mushroomed in 1990s on the ruins of the USSR. St. Petersburg’s administration was given the right to issue licenses on sales of the state resources (oil, precious and rare metals, etc.) and after the sales to foreign buyers went through, USD $122 million from these deals went missing. One of the first mentions of Vladimir Putin in the media was about these shady deals, which robbed St. Petersburg of the money needed to purchase food for the people — there were queues for bread in Russia at the time. There were many murders at the time in St. Petersburg with criminals and nouveau riches dividing the spheres of influence — and the KGB wasn’t uninvolved. In fact, the KGB used criminals to get control over money and assets — and then got rid of the criminal bosses after Putin’s accession to power in 2000. Krasikov is a privy to the wealth of secrets from these times — and likely the assassin behind many political liquidations on Putin’s direct orders, including the mysterious death of Putin’s former boss Anatoly Sobchak in February 2000 — weeks before Putin’s election as the President of Russia. Putin cannot afford the West to hold a key witness against him in a Hague trial — such secrets, if revealed, could mean the end of his legitimacy as the president of Russia in the eyes of the countries of “the global South” that still support him. That’s why Putin was willing to release 12 Russian political prisoners in exchange for Krasikov.

Question: Is it true that all of Russia is built on lies and deception? Vadim Krasikov, who was imprisoned in Germany for a murder of a former Chechen rebel leader in Berlin, worked for the Russian security service FSB, Putin admits. He previously denied this.
Answer: Apparently, Vadim Krasikov’s connection to Vladimir Putin goes back to 1990’s when he was a bodyguard for Putin during his time as Sobchak’s aide. Anatoly Sobchak with his aide Vladimir Putin. Vadim Krasikov became the only man among the released Russian agents whom Putin not only shook hands with, but also publicly hugged. Name: Elena Gold
Question: Russia has a history of throwing its citizens under the military wheel. What happens when the butcher's bill is too much for ordinary Russians? What happens when they realise, that in 2024, they don't have to die for a lunatic with an ego problem?
Answer: A Russian deserter who was tricked to sign up for the war told ‘The Insider’ how he was nearly killed by his own Russian troops at the front, next to a pit with 20–30 bodies. He was badly wounded when his commander sent him to pick some vodka, and nearly bled out with no assistance. It was after this experience that he decided to run off. Anton (not his real name) had no intention of joining the army whatsoever. But in the fall of 2023, he went out to a shop, and a police patrol stopped him to check his documents. Anton didn’t have his ID with him and the cops took him to the police station. They put his data into a computer and told him he had an outstanding mobilization summons and would be going to the front in 3 days. They threatened that he would have huge problems for trying to skip mobilization — but there could be a way around: he could go to the enlistment office and ask to sign the contract voluntarily. The cops told him that if he signed the contract (as opposed to being mobilized), he would be able to pick an “easy” job, like helping out in a hospital. Anton came home horrified. The idea of improving his odds to get an “easy” military job as opposed to being sent to the front as mobilized seemed reasonable. He decided that if he anyway would be mobilized, he’d better become a contractor. He signed the contract on Saturday, and on Tuesday he was already sent to a unit. And — surprise, surprise! — he was sent to an assault company. A week later he was already at the front line. That was a shock for Anton: “A week ago I was sitting at home, watching videos, working, leading a normal life, and now I'm at the trenches in Ukraine.” It didn’t take long at the front for commanders to start sending people to assaults. His unit’s goal was to take a position at the edge of a village. But to get there, the soldiers had to run over 500 meters of an open space. From the Ukrainian side, that open space was controlled by a machine gun that was able to take out up to 100 people at once. The only cover a group could take was a damaged tank stranded in the middle. The commander told the assault teams to take cover and dig an outpost near the tank, to create a position from which they would be able to move further forward. Anton says it was an idiotic plan: there was no difference whether you had to run 250 or 500 meters, after 30 seconds in an open area you would be a “toast”. The commander began sending groups of 5: on the first day, 4 groups were sent, all 20 ended up dead. No one could even reach that tank. The next day another 20 people got killed. Anton says, Ukrainians have 15–20 various drones — both killer drones and reconnaissance drones — in the air at any time, day or night. The drones see any movement immediately. “It felt like the Ukrainian Armed Forces had a 50-fold advantage in drones,” he says. Then the commanders decided to send only 2 people at once. One group managed to reach the tank and dug in, and the propagandists on TV immediately began reporting that “the village was taken.” But the Russian troops still haven’t even reached it. The commander, a former security guard from a supermarket, dreamed of seeing himself on Channel 1, to feel like a hero warrior. So, he kept sending one group after the other to the slaughter, demanding that they move forward towards the village. The group that dug in near the tank managed to survive, but they needed ammunition, food, water — so, more people were sent in to deliver supplies, and they kept being shot by the Ukrainian fire. Anton says that about 70 people died there in a week, near that tank. Anton says that the worst wasn’t even the gunfire — the worst was when you leave the dugout and are completely exposed, and you realize that at any second you can be killed. “I went out to the toilet, went back 30 seconds later, and at the place where I was, 2 mortars hit” he recalls. Sometimes the Ukrainian drone operators made errors and the drones fell down, then the commanders sent Russian soldiers into the minefields to pick them up. A task from which one is unlikely to return, because no one has maps of the minefields, the mines are just thrown in, where it falls, that’s where it falls. “You have a patch of land, 4 drones fly around it. They drop something, as soon as they fly away — the next 4 are already flying. And in the distance, there are probably 5 more, coordinating fire by mortars and artillery,” explains Anton. If a drone noticed you, you aren’t allowed to hide back in a dugout — because the operator sees a glowing dot, and suddenly it disappears: it means the person has gone somewhere. Then a precise hit arrives — and minimum 5 people in the dugout will be dead. Anton says that in 2 weeks, only 15–20 people were left from 250 soldiers that arrived, and from them 10 people were the commanders and non-combat clerks. Most of the soldiers were contractors, only a few were “mobilized”. From the losses, about 40% are dead, the rest are wounded. About 50% of the wounded are without legs or arms — disabled for life. “When I arrived, that village was still more or less intact. 3 weeks later it was just ruins. Heaps of corpses…” recalls Anton. He survived because he was part of the “evacuation team” — and he refused to go in the assaults, saying he would continue performing the task he was assigned to do. He was still going to the position near the tank, but his job was to pull the wounded, not carry provisions or stay in the dugout. Although Anton didn’t do any specific medical training, he had to perform an amputation in the field. This was like a horror movie. He pulled a guy who was lying wounded in the field for 3 days. The guy managed to apply tourniquets to wounds on his arm and leg, but after these 3 days his arm began to rot. The medics told him on the radio he had to amputate the arm. Anton injected the guy with all sedatives he could find and chopped the arm with an axe. It took him 4 attempts to get through the flesh and bones, then he had to treat the stump and bandage it. “I didn't sleep for two days after that,” Anton says. “When we were loading him [for evacuation], he was still alive, and he also made it to the first line alive. I don't know what happened to him after that.” Another guy that Anton pulled out had part of his jaw torn off, his arm up to the shoulder and half a leg. The commander was pissed off about it: "I don't need this, now I have to do something for one more person." A day later the injured guy was already begging to die, realizing he wouldn’t survive. At the end, he bled to death. The dead were rarely pulled out from the field. It was too much trouble to even attempt it. Once Anton had to hide from a drone and crawled into an old dugout, and realized he was crawling on top of liquified bodies in uniform. The bodies were there for already 3–4 months. There was one guy in the unit of about 18–19, he was a draftee (all Russian men have to serve a 1-year compulsory military service, but the draftees are not supposed to be sent to Ukraine to the war). That guy was also tricked into signing a contract — in the military enlistment office where he arrived as a draftee, they simply gave him some papers to sign, and he signed, not realizing what it was. “A week and a half later, he was already at the front line,” says Anton. The guy’s family sent a letter, complaining to the prosecutor's office that he was forced to sign the contract. The battalion commander was furious about it and gave the order to “sort him out.” The teenage soldier was sent into an attack and killed within a week. Anton says his commander was constantly drunk. One day the commander ordered him to pick another drone from the headquarters — Anton argued it was unnecessary to do it at night, as they had a spare drone they could use, and at night it’s really easy to see a person on thermal visors. But the commander insisted. Anton managed to get to the headquarters, where they gave him a drone and a package “for the commander”. Anton looked inside the bag, and there were bottles of vodka and cognac. The commander sent him to get the alcohol for him and he didn’t care it was deadly dangerous. On the way back, Anton heard a drone over him and immediately an explosive dropped on him. Anton was wounded and couldn’t walk, but he realized he still had both his arms and legs. He threw away the bag with vodka and crawled into the nearest basement, got on the radio, said that he was wounded and asked for evacuation. They responded it was too dangerous to try to get him. After 20 minutes, he realized that he was bleeding out. “I was shaking all over, tremors, I definitely lost a liter of blood,” says Anton. He decided to crawl, and managed to make it to the line where he could be picked up — out of the firing range. Anton says that ”almost everyone drinks” at the front line — or they are using cheap drugs (“salts”). The commanders also steal strong pain killers from the first aid kits given to soldiers and use those. If a soldier refuses to follow orders, he isn’t sent to a military court for prosecution but simply shot by the commander’s underlings — his arms and legs are taped to a tree, and he’s shot at a point blank range. Sometimes a person may be dressed in 2 bulletproof vests and then shot at with a machine gun, his ribs get broken and he slowly dies. Or he’s shot at through a helmet — such shots take off the whole skull. Anton says that 2 soldiers in his unit were liquidated like this, for not following orders — they refused to go in an attack, because all previous groups were killed. Anton himself nearly got shot — when in the field, he noticed a drone in the sky and went back, but took to the left and ended up in a neighboring unit. That unit was looking for a mobilized soldier on the run and took Anton for the deserter. He was tied to a tree and about to be shot, there was a hole nearby, where 20–30 bodies were already lying. He was saved by a radio message that the runaway soldier was found. Do the Russian soldiers realize that Russia’s war in Ukraine is evil? Do they blame Putin for that? Nobody among the Russian troops at the front says things like "let's go overthrow Putin,” states Anton. “Of course, they say that he [Putin] has started some kind of screwup that no one needs.” ”Even the ‘patriots’ when they arrive, very soon start saying, ‘What are we even doing here, why the heck do we need this?’” “There are some ‘ultra patriots’, but they do not survive for long, because they are the first to run ahead and the first to get killed.” “There was this guy, 54 years old, his wife had cancer. He came not even for the money, but because he needed the benefits for a serviceman's family, so his wife could get the cancer treatment. He was saying: ‘I know that people get killed here, I made my choice. If I get killed, at least my wife will get 5 million ruble, she will get the treatment, the children will live well." That guy lived in a small regional town. His monthly salary was 35,000 ruble (about USD$400). He had 3 kids, his wife was sick. He saw it as his only option to help the wife and the kids. “You are not a human being there at all,” says Anton. He fears what is going to happen in Russia when all these people with the broken psyche come back. “When these people come back from the war with blood on their hands, with a broken psyche, who were in the same companies, detachments and so on, they will start to form groups, and these smaller groups will start to form bigger groups...” Anton says that plenty of weapons are transported back to Russia in bags with dead bodies — pulled into parts and hidden in these bags. An AK-47 costs about 40,000 ruble in Russia now ($460). Anton says that if the Russian soldiers are being utilized at the same rate as at his part of the front, Russia has suffered about 400,000 losses by now — killed and badly wounded. Anton says that no one signing an army contract should hope they’d come back with the money — because they won’t. At best, they can hope to come back home with the money in case of a serious wound — but then, “Do you want your mother to be wiping off your butt for the rest of your life?” “If you think there are some Nazis there... There are no Nazis, there are ordinary people. If you, so to say, go and kill your neighbor, would you be able to live with that for the rest of your life?” “This war is not worth it. This is not a war for the Fatherland, this is not a war for justice, not a war for freedom — this is a war for the complete bullshit. A war for the grandfather who is so crazy that he went and killed hundreds of thousands of people for nothing, just like that.” “You are not liberating anyone. He [the crazy grandfather] himself doesn't believe that he is liberating anyone, he doesn't give a f**k about all this — and even less about you.” What can the Russian men do to avoid being sent to the war? “Better run,” says Anton. ”No money? Take out loans and use that money to escape.” Anton himself deserted after getting wounded. Yesterday, Putin signed a decree raising the federal payout on signing the army contact to 400,000 rub. ($4,600) — it’s nearly twice as much as the state was paying before. Regions are also raising their payouts — St. Petersburg just raised it’s top-up to 1.8 million, and Moscow already lifted it to 1.9 million rub. ($22,000). Russia is running out of volunteers, so the prices for cannon fodder are rising. Putin is too scared to do another mobilization and force people to kill and die, because he knows how unpopular this war really is.

Question: What do you make of the fact that Paul Whelan was left out of the prisoner exchange between the US and Russia?
Answer: In December 2022, Paul Whelan wasn’t part of a prisoner exchange between Russia and the U.S. — instead, American basketball player Brittney Greener was traded for Russian arms dealer Victor Bout. Putin managed to get his “merchant of death” Bout back, releasing an American hostage Griner who was arrested in Russia for carrying vaporizer cartridges containing less than a gram of hash oil. Maybe this time Paul Whelan will also be released.

Question: During the Red Terror and Stalin's later purges, what made one end up on the kill lists? How could one protect oneself from ending up dead or in the Gulag?
Answer: On July 30, 1937, the NKVD of the USSR signed order No. 00447. This was the start of Stalin's "Great Terror." “The Kulak Operation” targeted those whom Stalin’s regime considered “class enemies”: former kulaks (well-off peasants), former nobility, former members of “anti-Soviet parties", former White Army officers, pre-1917 civil servants, church officials, people with links to foreign countries (Germans, Estonians, Finns, etc.), and other "socially undesirable elements". In the next 400 days, hundreds of thousands of people were killed, millions sent to GULAG. About 700,000 people were shot, after they signed confessions that they planned to damage the Soviet state — signed under torture. More than 1.7 million people were arrested and given various prison terms; hundreds of thousands of them never returned from the GULAG. There were no trials, not even an appearance of trials. Instead, the NKVD gave the power to sentence people to death or decades of GULAG to "special trios." “The trio” included the head of the local NKVD, the head of the regional communist party committee, and the prosecutor. The accused didn’t have attorneys. There were no lawyers. There was no public. Just the accused, the trio, and the prison guards. Sentences were given within minutes, one by one: guilty. The Soviet conveyor of death. Some death lists were approved by Stalin himself. The USSR dictator personally sanctioned the execution of more than 40,000 people. There were already purges in the first half of the 1930s: in 1934, 80,000 people were convicted in OGPU-NKVD cases. And let’s not forget the man-made famines of 1932–33 that killed millions. Many thought that the purge would not affect them, that the NKVD came for ”saboteurs” and “spies” — that if you were a model citizen, obeying every Stalin’s order, satisfying all his whims, then you would be okay. And then suddenly millions of these “model citizens” found themselves signing “admissions of guilt” under horrendous torture. Their wives were either shot or sent to GULAG, as were their teenage children. Minor kids were sent to orphanages or adopted by families of other law-obedient Soviet citizens. Kids of “enemies of the state”. No names — just numbers. Stalin didn’t invent “The Red Terror”. It was invented by Vladimir Lenin — the father of October 1917 Bolsheviks’ coup. Lenin ordered to kill anyone who was against “the proletarian revolution”. And anyone who potentially could be against it — just in case. The horror of the Red Terror is realistically conveyed in the Russian-made film "Chekist" (1992). It should have been shown to Russian schoolkids. It wasn’t. Now it’s too late and Putin’s goons won’t allow it. Putin’s goons are making a hero and “the father of the nation” out of Stalin, erect monuments to him. Hundreds of thousands of Russian men are sent to slaughter in Ukraine — 1,000 of them are ending dead, maimed or wounded every single day. And these men came to Ukraine to kill people who simply lived their life on their land, and they came because of the hatred with which Putin’s goons poisoned their minds and souls. And all these Russian citizens of today behave like the Soviet citizens of 1930s, they are sure that if they are being “good patriots”, they will be okay. Russia is falling into the same pattern. Again.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What's wrong with most Russian people?
Answer: An old man in Bashkortostan is being sent to war, from which he is unlikely to return. Well-groomed, well-dressed officials are standing there and sending an elderly man, who clearly was forced to sign a contract because the family needs the money, to a nearly certain death. His family and friends — 2 women to the left and 2 men to the right — are also there to say ‘Good bye.” And no one is ashamed to look the poor guy in the eye. The head of the administration of the Kiginsky district posted the photo that shows the whole essence of the recruitment of volunteers. ”Thank you for your courage! Wishing you strength, luck and health, to return home safe and sound!” wrote Ruslan Vakhitov. If Vakhitov doesn’t send the allocated number of “volunteers”, he’d be in a big trouble with his superiors — delivering enough “cannon fodder” is #1 responsibility of every head of administration in 2024 Russia. Bashkiria pays 1 million rub. (USD 11,000) on sign up of an army contract — in Moscow, volunteers are paid twice as much. (Original screenshot in the comments below.) That’s how much the life of a Russian citizen is worth – $10,000–24,000, depending on the place of residence. The government pays more for the life of a Muscovite than for a resident of small Siberian towns. Young Russian men who emigrated with their wives to avoid mobilization say their mothers wanted them to go to war — even tried to report them to the military enlistment office, to stop them from leaving Russia. The oppositional Russian media outlet ‘Meduza’ tells stories of 2 men whose mothers wanted them to go to war: they wanted their sons to be “heroes” — even if the sons would be killed. The guys say the biggest motivation of their mothers wasn’t even the money — it was their own social status. Mothers were more concerned what others would think than the well-being of their sons. Sergey’s story When Russia began its mobilization campaign in the fall of 2022, Sergey protested by putting up anti-war posters. He was arrested, and after his release, he decided to emigrate with his wife and 1-year-old son. He didn’t tell his parents about it: they were avid supporters of Putin. Sergey purchased tickets and exchanged funds from rubles to dollars. It was the currency exchange receipt that his mother accidentally found — and began asking questions. Sergey told his mother they planned to leave in 2 months (they were leaving sooner, but he was hesitant to reveal the exact date, fearing that his mother might try to physically stop them). The mother was furious: ‘Why don’t you want to go defend your country? You owe it!’” Sergey was evasive, and his mother was getting more and more agitated. “It’s your duty! You’re a man! Come on — you don’t even have a good job right now! You’ll make some money, you’ll be a hero, and your son will be proud of you!” When Sergey asked whether she realized that he could be killed, she responded that “at least you’d die like a man.” “Everyone will be proud of you. Your son will see you as a hero, and your wife will be the widow of a hero.” This was so weird that Sergey didn’t even take his mother’s words seriously. But she was dead serious. She even summoned his younger brother to inform the military enlistment office about Sergey’s plans to skip the draft. “Go to the conscription office and turn him in, so that he doesn’t escape,” she instructed the younger brother. Sergey couldn’t believe it — his brother had to send him the screenshots of correspondence with the mother. Grigory’s story Grigory is also a young father. His daughter was born shortly before February 2022. When Russia began mobilization in September 2022, he decided to leave the country. When he told his mother on the phone that he was planning to leave with the wife and their child, she demanded that he’d go and fight in Ukraine. “Grigory, why would you leave? That’s a felony! Why don’t you just go, try it out?” demanded his mother. “Who knows — maybe you’ll even come back,” she added chillingly. These last words shocked the young father. “I couldn’t believe it at first,” Grigory says. “I said we had a bad connection and asked her to repeat what she’d said. Then I gave the phone to my wife, and my mother said the same thing to her.” His wife’s parents had the same opinion: they wanted their son-in-law to go to war. His mother-in-law insisted that Grigory should “go and defend his homeland”. When he asked his mother what if he were killed, she just wouldn’t respond. “What could she say? That she wouldn’t be sorry to see her own son be killed for no reason?” Grigory commented bitterly. His wife also asked his mother if she weren’t worried to lose her son, and the mother responded that “everyone is going” — and that his wife should let him go, too, because he “might return.” “The only thing she was thinking about was the social status it would supposedly bring. Based on her personality, I think she was just afraid of what people would say,” Grigory concludes. The present Both Sergey and Grigory left Russia. They now live abroad. They didn’t completely cut off communication with their parents, but the relationship is extremely strained. Basically, they only call to allow the kids chat to their grandparents. Grigory says he feels better now about the whole thing, although at first it did affect him. Sergey still talks to his father, who supports the war but didn’t try to stop him from leaving. “But not my mom: she’s blacklisted forever,” he says. “It was painful to learn that my mother wishes me dead… It was pretty hard to come to terms with the fact that the person who carried me inside her, who washed my butt when I was little, can just say: go die. But what am I losing by not seeing my mother? She didn’t have any kind of special motherly love for me. All I’m losing is the physical presence of a person who only yells at me, curses at me, and is always upset about something. And who spouted crazy fascist nonsense every day,” Sergey concludes.

Question: Was Stalin really that bad, or was he a victim of propaganda?
Answer: In 1930s, young Mikhail Sholokhov was already a known author in the USSR for his book “Tales of the Don” (1925), depicting his personal experiences during the WWI, the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 and the Civil War. When Stalin’s attack on peasants with the goal of shoveling them into “collective farms” began, Sholokhov lived in the village of Veshenskaya, Rostov region, and could see what was happening with the people. Witnessing the deaths and suffering of peasants, Sholokhov wrote 4 letters to Stalin in hopes of saving people. April 20, 1932: “I saw something that cannot be forgotten till my last days: at night, in the Volokhovsky village of the Lebyazhensky collective farm, in the fierce wind, in the freezing cold, when even dogs were hiding from the frosty weather, families of peasants who were thrown out of their houses had been burning fires in the alleys and sitting near the flames. Children were wrapped in rags and laid on the bare ground, thawed by the fire. A continuous children’s cry stood over the alleys. Why are people being tortured like that? In the Bazkovsky collective farm, a woman with a baby was evicted from her home. She was walking around the village all night, asking to be allowed to warm up with her child. Nobody let her in, fearing that if they do, they themselves would be evicted. By morning, the child froze to death in his mother's arms...” Stalin replied that Sholokhov simply lacked the class consciousness. Yes, Stalin was absolutely evil. It’s not just “propaganda”.

Question: How is the Russian economy doing? What kind of data has its economy produced in recent months, positive or negative?
Answer: From January 2020 to May 2024, inflation in Russia is double the G7 average. Russia’s central bank had to raise its base interest rate from 7.5% in June 2023 to 16% in June 2024 — and in July 2024, it was increased by 200 basis points at once — to 18% per annum. So, Russia’s base interest rate is 3% higher than in Afghanistan. There are no plans to reduce the key rate this year, stated Elvira Nabiullina, head of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation. She added that the rate will remain high for a long time, and an additional increase is possible. Thank the glorious leader Vladimir Putin for that. (Video in the comments below.) If anyone saw the devastation of “the rest of Russia”, this certainly sounds like a threat rather than an optimistic forecast. And it’s highly doubtful that Russia is capable to quickly bring back to life the destroyed Ukrainian cities. Mariupol, Bakhmut, Avdeevka, Marinka — these Ukrainian cities had their own thriving identities before the war — Russia put on them the mangled masks of the “Russian world.” The ruins are visible on Google Planet, from satellites. In the past weeks, Russia got hit by rolling blackouts — in Krasnodar region, people went to the streets to protest, after not having power and water for several days — the water supply was switched off because there was no power. There are rumors of an accident at a nuclear power station near Rostov, and as a result, insufficient power produced to supply the nearby regions. The “new regions” — how Putin calls the occupied Ukrainian territories — are getting the power from Russia; before the occupation, they were getting the electricity from Ukraine. The Russian grid hadn’t been maintained and repaired properly due to the lack of funds (the money is spent on the war in Ukraine) and western sanctions (parts aren’t easily accessible — and Russia doesn’t make them). Russia is stuck in Ukraine and the money is disappearing in the black hole of the war, with nothing but ruined cities to show for that. And these ruined cities will require an enormous investment to bring them back to life — and who’s going to invest in a territory that’s occupied and can change its citizenship or be bombed to ruins tomorrow? “Russians will have many more troubles because the country is worn out. It was necessary to close Russia down for the major renovation for about 10 years. Then it would’ve been possible to live through the 21st century normally. Instead of that, the country was sent to war,” says Igor Lipsits, a prominent Russian economist and founder of the Higher School of Economics in Moscow, who was forced to emigrate because of his critical stance. The Russian economy is in a state of flux. The western sanctions suffocate it slowly but surely — and this is why Putin keeps demanding the lifting of western sanctions as a condition of a “peace agreement”. Because Russia is screwed unless the sanctions are lifted — no matter what is the situation on the ground in Ukraine. There is really no good scenario for the Russian economy — its down spiral is irreversible at this point. It’s like a worn off car — it requires a complete rebuild to operate properly again.

Question: Are there any specific stories within the 100 Ukrainians released from Russian captivity that you found particularly moving?
Answer: Here is this story that I cried reading. You might cry, too. A guy tells his mother after being released from captivity: “We didn’t believe in the exchange until the very end. Because they deceived us so much, they tormented us... They would take us for executions and for exchanges... And then they would bring us back and laugh at us. And when a soldier came into the bus and said, "You’re home, boys, Glory to Ukraine!" - I just started breathing; I hadn't been breathing, Mom, really. And when we saw people along the road greeting us with flags, flowers, and signs, it felt like a movie, like it wasn’t happening to us. And then, when we finally arrived, the first cigarette, hugs, they gave us a phone, I forgot your number, Mom, can you imagine? But you’re not mad, because how could I forget your number? I repeated it to myself for 2 years. Like you taught me in childhood - "My name is...., I live at..., Mom’s phone number is...." The boys cried, but I didn't. And at the hospital, they gave us clothes and took us to the dining room. And there was food, Mom. There were 3 bowls of different things for each of us. I don’t know, I didn’t eat that much in captivity in a month. And the smell of the soup. My head started spinning. The bowl was so deep, the soup was up to the brim. I was so careful with the spoon, trying not to spill anything, but my hands were shaking, Mom, because I wanted to eat properly, but I also wanted to just grab the bowl and drink it all. And my hands were shaking. And oh, how much I wanted to eat, you can’t imagine. And I was so careful, trying to be proper... A lady walked around, refilling everything for us, she came up to me, hugged me, stroked my head like Grandma used to, kissed me on the temple - "Eat, dear, I’ll bring more," she said. And that’s when I cried. I ate and cried, afraid to look up because I felt ashamed. And then I looked around, and almost all of us were like that - eating and crying. And the soup, Mom, I’ve never had anything tastier in my life. You’re not upset, are you, Mom?”

Question: Why do Russians let Putin do what he does?
Answer: Back in 1998, when Vladimir Putin was made the director of the FSB, Anatoly Levin-Utkin, a journalist of the newspaper “Legal Petersburg”, co-authored an article that said it was illegal — Putin had no right to head the FSB, because he was a lieutenant colonel, not a general. The article featured in print the first extensive biography of the future Russian president and his connections to various power brokers. It also mentioned the investigation of the city council commission into contracts of 1991-1992 for rare metals and petroleum products supplied as barter in exchange to goods. As a result of that investigation, which found huge issues, deputies requested Putin to resign from his post of the head of the committee dealing with foreign companies. A week after the publication of the article, Levin-Utkin was brutally murdered at the entrance of his apartment building. He was beaten to death with a metal rod. Soon, the newspaper that published that article, ceased to exist as well. In 1990s, Vladimir Putin was very much a part of “Bandit Petersburg” as a connection between the city administration and organized criminal groups, and when he moved to Moscow after he mismanaged the re-election campaign of his boss, St. Petersburg mayor Anatoly Sobchak (who also died under strange circumstances shortly thereafter), he still had connections that would “make problems disappear” on his request. And after Putin became the chief of the FSB, he created a department of assassins who now not only kill people inside Russia, but also travel the world, poisoning the targets picked by Putin (Litvinenko, Skripals), or incapacitate them (the infamous Havana syndrome). Putin is a sadistic murderer and he rules Russia by torturing and murdering his critics and political opponents. He’s in charge of the same machine that Stalin used to kill 60 million of his own citizens. That’s why millions of Russian citizens left Russia during the time of Putin in power. I left Russia before Putin became the president, but I’ve met many Russians who chose to leave because of Putin’s criminal policies.

Question: How high are Russian salaries in general?
Answer: According to Russian statistics, the average monthly salary (after tax) in Russia is USD $648. It’s lower than in Mexico, but higher than in India. In 2013, before Putin’s annexation of Crimea, the average monthly salary in Russia was over $1,000, and in China it was $650. Now it’s the other way around. But $648 per month isn’t what the majority of Russians earn. The median wage in Russia is only 46,000 rub. (about $500). And half of the population of Russia are earning less than $500 per month. Wages and one-time payouts on sign up for those willing to go to Ukraine to kill Ukrainians keep rising. Right now, in St. Petersburg, the willing cannon fodder is paid 1.3 million rub. (USD $15,000) on sign up — that’s what a median wage earner gets in 2 years and 4 months. The monthly wage on offer is 210,000 rub. ($2,400) — that’s 5 time more than the official Russian median salary (real Russian wages are lower; Rosstat uses a lot of statistical tricks to remove low wage earners from the calculations). The Russian state tempts poverty-stricken Russians, offering them a chance to earn “big money” and buy a car or a home — totally unaffordable for them on their regular wages. Meanwhile, in Russia, since July 1, interest rates on loans for used cars have been lifted to 27%, and for new cars to 24%. Interest rates on home loans are on average at 19.69%. Russia struggles to sell its gas after losing the European market — but hey, we can charge Russian citizens more! Meanwhile, these are apparently the salaries of Russia’s leading propagandists: Somehow, Margarita Simonyan is missing on the list. Question: What are some weird facts about the USSR and living in the Communist Soviet Union?

The purpose of the purge was to destroy any possible resistance to the totalitarian Soviet regime ruled by Joseph Stalin. These are the photos taken by the NKVD, the Soviet secret service, of innocent people they were about to execute. All the people in these photos were shot in basements after confessing under torture in various heinous crimes — spying for Japan, China or France, plotting to assassinate Stalin, and so on. All the people in these photos were “rehabilitated” after Stalin’s death (declared innocent). The families of those shot didn’t know their loved ones were dead. For years, they were sending them parcels with food, cigarettes, warm clothing — when they themselves didn’t have enough to eat and wore the same clothes for years. The relatives of the victims were coming to the department of prisons and standing in queues for hours to send parcels, tolerating abuse and mockery from the guards. You don’t need to guess where the contents of these parcels went. It’s only after Stalin’s death they found out that the sentence of “10 years without correspondence” meant that the person was shot on the same day. In addition to 1.1 million people who were shot, 4.5 million of USSR citizens were sent to remote GULAG camps for terms of minimum of 10 years, sentenced to hard labor. Many of them died before they got there — getting sick in cattle train carriages, during long marches to the “camps”, many others died later in the camps because of deceases, starvation, freezing cold, exhaustion, or took their own lives. Women often were raped to death on arrival to a prison camp, after a queue of hardened male prisoners were given access by prison guards in exchange for a pack of cigarettes. Meanwhile, the rest of Soviet citizens pretended that nothing was happening, that life was great, and becoming better with every year. The black NKVD cars were arriving at night and quickly grabbing the whole family, by morning the apartment was empty, as if no one ever lived there. And the neighbors weren’t asking questions because they didn’t want the black car to pick them up the next night. That’s the country that Vladimir Putin wants to restore.

Question: What do you think will happen to Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich who was arrested for alleged spying in Russia?
Answer: On July 19, 2024, the Regional Court in Yekaterinburg, Russia, sentenced American journalist Evan Gershkovich to 16 years in a maximum security colony. Russian human rights activist Vladimir Osechkin says that possibly he was baited by the FSB, to facilitate his arrest. 32-year-old journalist of WSJ was found guilty of espionage for collecting information about ‘Uralvagonzavod’, which is a factory that makes tanks for the Russian army. The prosecutor asked for an 18-year sentence. Gershkovich pleaded “not guilty” and insisted that he was acting as a journalist, not a spy. The court hearings were held behind closed doors, as the prosecution alleged the information that Gershkovich was getting was a “state secret”. Only the judge, the prosecutor, the defendant and his lawyers were present. Journalists were allowed into the meeting room for a few minutes before the hearing commenced to take photos and videos. Gershkovich, with a shaved head, greeted his colleagues with a smile, but did not answer any questions. Journalists were also allowed into the courtroom for the announcement of the harsh verdict: 16 years in a maximum security prison. Evan Gershkovich was detained on March 29, 2023 in Yekaterinburg, where he arrived for the second time in a month, to continue his investigation for the next story. At the WSJ Gershkovich worked since January 2022 — he joined the respected media just a month before Russia invaded Ukraine. Since then, he authored several key news stories related to Russia and Ukraine. In early March 2023, weeks before his arrest in Russia, he and his colleagues released a story about the growing tensions between the founder of “Wagner” Yevgeny Prigozhin and the Kremlin elites. In particular, the material stated, Kremlin officials turned to Russian President Vladimir Putin with a request to “rein in” Prigozhin, who criticized the Russian Ministry of Defense. Gershkovich was also one of the authors of a high-profile WSJ article about how Putin’s entourage may be hiding truthful information from him about the war in Ukraine. Putin receives a written report from the front every morning, however, the reports emphasize Russia army’s successes, and failures are tuned down. The reports are also delayed for several days, because they have to pass filters of the FSB and the Security Council, as well as get a personal stamp of approval from Nikolai Patrushev (then the secretary of Russia’s Security Council), the article claimed. Gershkovich's materials before his arrest in March 2023 were devoted to the worsening prospects for the Russian economy, the situation around Bakhmut, the visit to Moscow of China’s leader Xi Jinping and protests over the bill on "foreign agents" in Georgia. According to the photographer who worked with Gershkovich, he was collecting material for an article about how people in Russian regions perceive the war, for which he visited Yekaterinburg and Nizhny Tagil, and planned to go to other cities. The media wrote that Gershkovich was also interested in activities of the “Wagner”, including recruitment and cemeteries of the deceased fighters. At his court process, Gershkovich did not admit guilt and insisted that his research was purely journalistic. Evan Gershkovich became the first American journalist in modern Russian history to be accused of espionage. The last time an American journalist had been detained in Russia on espionage charges was in 1986, when a “News & World Report” employee Nicholas Daniloff was arrested. Daniloff was exchanged 3 weeks later. Before his arrest, Gershkovich worked in Russia for about 6 years, since 2017. At the time of his detainment, he had been living in London but regularly traveled on business trips to Russia, where he worked as part of the WSJ's Moscow bureau. His parents Mikhail Gershkovich and Emma Milman were emigrants from the USSR, but Evan himself lived his entire life in America. Several journalists who were friends with Gershkovich said that they warned him that reporting in Russia on the topics he was picking was dangerous and he could be arrested. But obviously, he didn’t think so. Gershkovich’s name has been frequently mentioned as someone who could be exchanged to Russian spies and assassins, arrested in Europe and the USA. He is probably the highest profile American hostage held by Putin. Putin discussed exchanging Gershkovich in his interview to Tucker Carlson in February 2024. Putin wanted to get in exchange the FSB assassin Vadim Krasikov, who is imprisoned in Germany. In 2021, Vadim Krasikov was sentenced to life in prison for the murder of Chechen field commander Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin in 2019. Carlson said at the time that Putin needed to talk to Germans about it. Peculiarly, Gershkovich’s process wasn’t held in Moscow but 2 thousand kilometers away, in Yekaterinburg, where he was arrested — away from Russia’s capital, where most of the foreign correspondents reside. This obviously prevented many western ambassadors and embassy officials from attending the process, which they would likely do as a show of solidarity, if the court hearing was in Moscow. The only hope for Gershkovich to get out of the Russian prison is an agreement for an exchange, which Putin would probably only approve if his assassin Krasikov is released, and Germany doesn’t seem keen on that. Otherwise, Gershkovich may only hope to get out if Vladimir Putin, on whose order he was arrested (no doubt, such high profile arrest and prosecution would require the highest nod), is no longer the ruler of Russia. So, Gershkovich is likely to remain behind bars in Russia, as the locals call it, “for as long as Putin is alive.”

Question: Why isn't Russia sending its best military (drone, jets) to dominate Ukraine? Is Putin intentionally sending its weakest force?

Question: Why do Americans so like to kill their presidents? How many of them were killed?

Question: What was it like in the USSR between the 1991 coup d'état attempt and the dissolution of the Soviet Union?
Answer: The August 1991 coup by ‘GKChP’ (State Committee on Emergency Situation) — formed by die-hard communists who were against democratic changes introduced by the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev — shocked the USSR citizens to the core. In these 3 days from August 19 to 21 people feared that their newfound freedoms — most notably, freedom of private entrepreneurship and freedom of speech — would be again taken away from them by the communists. This is why thousands of people came to the central squares of the cities — to defend what they’ve just got. People liked the new life more than the old, pre-1985 life. When the coup was defeated and its participants arrested, people breathed a sigh of relief. But their problems didn’t disappear. There was still shortage of food in the country. December 14, 1991, ‘In The Queue’ (independent newspaper): “Ukraine sends ham and sugar to Russia. The government of the capital begins to privatize shops. There will be no hunger — there will be enough potatoes and flour for the whole of winter.” This newspaper was published 6 days after the Belovezha Accords were signed on December 8, 1991, declaring that the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) had effectively ceased to exist. On December 12, the Supreme Soviet of the Russian SFSR formally ratified the Belovezha Accords, denounced the 1922 Treaty on the Creation of the Soviet Union, and recalled the Russian deputies from the Supreme Soviet of the USSR. GKChP sped up the process of the Soviet republics wanting to separate from the abusive treatment by Moscow. But the leaders of Russia (which was only 1 of 15 Soviet Republics) also didn’t want the USSR anymore — and the Soviet people were weary of the return of “the classic communism”. That’s why no one really cared when the USSR ceased to exist. It was strange, weird, yet kind of unimportant — the important people, like leaders of each republic, were still on charge. So, people just moved on with their lives, without thinking twice, and started to get ready to celebrate Christmas and the New Year’s Eve. The giant 70-year-old country stopped existing — and people carried on, as of nothing happened. That was truly remarkable.
