The doctor agreed with my wife and also agreed with me that Lenin was an abhorrent individual. Finding no reason to take me to the psychiatric ward, the team left. Then an agitated guy from the National Guard came, made demands, took photos and yelled. What did he want was unclear, and I thought that the orderlies had left too early, because the National Guard guy clearly needed help. Then the criminal investigator came and immediately decided to send me to prison for a year, right from the first sentence. I was talking to him as nice as I could, but at some point he began swearing, calling me a “navalnist” and “an enemy of the people.” He shouted that under Putin, life was only getting better every year, that people at the top knew better what should be done. However, tired of his own propaganda, the guy began demanding me to unlock my phone, I refused, he yelled some more – and then abruptly left. A couple of hours later, they gave me 20.2 — holding a solo protest — expectedly, lied in their protocols. My court trial is in a week. Then they demanded from me to take off my T-shirt, because now it was “evidence”. I took it off — I had a spare one. The spare one had a peace sign on it. All the policemen (5 people) looked at each other questioningly. The criminal investigator was the first to stir and shout: “So, you’re a hippie, I didn’t get it right away! Ok, go ahead, you can wear this T-shirt.” The older guy didn’t believe him and decided to ring the anti-extremism center, who okayed the “hippie clothes.” As he was taking me outside, the police boss added that an inscription “I am against Stalin” is also prohibited. “He won the war” — that was his reasoning.” 2017: Alexey Sokirko with an anti-Putin poster. (Image is translated by Google Translate, the original image in the comments below.) In February 2024, Sokirko was arrested for laying flowers at the “Wall of Sorrow” — the memorial to victims of political repressions in Moscow that Voldemort Pootin would gladly demolish. It was on February 17, the next day after the news of Alexei Navalny’s death in an Arctic prison became known. At the police department, Sokirko was given a warning “not to break the law” and released. (As if laying flowers at a memorial was a crime.) “On my way out of the police station, I asked if I could go to Navalny’s funeral,” Sokirko wrote. An employee of the Anti-Extremism Center replied, “You have several kids, think about your family.” ”I’m thinking about my family and that’s why I would be going to the funeral,” stated defiant activist. Over the past 1.5 years, Russian courts sent at least 33 defendants in political cases to forced psychiatric treatment. It’s not as many as during the times of the USSR (detention in psychiatric wards was a popular method of suppressing dissent — people were more terrified of being turned into vegetables by injection of psychotic drugs than of being locked in a prison), but Putin’s regime is already using this measure 5 times more often than during the pre-war years. North Korea, here we come.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How can I join Russian Army as a foreigner? I know I need to know Russian. Do I need to be a resident or not? Tell me all requirements for it.
Answer: “They went on the assault, and the commanders shouted to them, “Quickly! Fast! Forward!” And everyone died…” Jaroslav Halajczyk is a citizen of Slovakia. Living in the European Union, in a NATO country, he was fascinated by the distant Russia and “mysterious Russian soul.” He thought that moving to a hut somewhere in the forests of Siberia, away from civilization, would be an awesome idea. Yaroslav’s romantic ideas about Russia nearly got him killed, but he was lucky. Name: Elena Gold
Question: Why is Orban so pro-Russian?
Answer: Bottom photo: Miklos Horthy, regent of the Kingdom of Hungary in 1920-1944 with Adolf Hitler. Top photo: Vladimir Putin with Victor Orbán, prime minister of Hungary since 2010. After an unannounced visit to Kyiv to meet president Zelenskyy on July 2, Orbán “suddenly” decided to fly to Moscow on July 5 for personal talks with Vladimir Putin. Kremlin’s speaker Dmitry Peskov denied that Orbán’s visit was planned before the Hungarian president went to meet with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, and insisted that Orbán’s request to visit Moscow only arrived on July 3. (And we know what it means when Peskov is denying something.) In the meeting with Orbán, Putin repeated his ridiculous ultimatum for Ukraine to surrender 4 regions (within their administrative boundaries) to Russia, which he first verbalized in mid-June, days before the Swiss Global Peace Summit, organized by Ukraine. Surely, for Orbán it was a shock, because just a day before in Astana (Kazakhstan), Putin was saying that Russia would be happy with the outline of the preliminary draft agreement achieved between the Russian and Ukrainian delegations in March 2022 in Istanbul, which had absolutely different conditions. What could be the reason for Putin’s sudden “change of heart”? Maybe 2 or more reasons are correct. For starters, Putin said that he was talking to Orbán as the chairman of the European Union — the formal position that Hungary took from July 1 — and Putin’s ridiculous ultimatum was to the EU. Obviouslty, Orbán had no authority from the EU to negotiate with Putin — he was too chicken to even inform the EU that he was flying to Moscow. When the news about the visit spread, Polish leader asked Orbán in disbelief if it were true. So, Putin used Orbán like a pawn, luring him to Moscow with a prospect of becoming a “peacemaker” — and then sacrificing him to paint a picture for his serfs, positioning himself as a victorious leader who is visited by the chairman of the EU begging to stop the war. Not only Orbán was unsuccessful in convincing Zelenskyy to announce a ceasefire, but he was treated by Putin as a whipping boy, allowing the Kremlin tyrant to elevate his own status among the local patriots and lift the spirits of Russian soldiers, who only want to get back home alive. As Russia’s widely advertised “Kharkiv offensive” stalled, Putin’s calls for “peace negotiations” amplified. Which of course wouldn’t be happening if Putin’s situation was advantageous and he had good prospects. Putin is facing a bottomless abyss, and that’s the only reason he keeps asking for “peace” — which Russians could have any day if they simply withdrew their troops from Ukraine. But Putin never wanted peace — if he did, he would have never invaded. Putin wants his troops to have carte blanche to do whatever they wish on the occupied Ukrainian territories — and do it with impunity. Putin needs to present a victory to the Russian population that’s growing increasingly tired of the war and angry about their own worsening situation. Putin needs to save the Russian economy from collapse, and for the western sanctions to be lifted, before Russia turns into a cold-climate version of North Korea. P.S. Orban left just hours before Hurricane Orkhan hit the Russian capital. A fateful omen.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How does the arrest of Laurent Vinatier, a French researcher who was charged with violating the "foreign agents" law in Russia, affect international relations?
Answer: Laurent Vinatier, a French researcher who was charged with violating the "foreign agents" law, was arrested in Russia and sent to pre-trial detention on June 7, 2024. Yesterday, he appeared in a Moscow court for a hearing, asking to be allowed to stay under house arrest, but his request was denied by the judge. Vinatier seemed a shadow of his confident self from a month ago. He appeared at the hearing via a video link. The French consul general in Moscow was present at the hearing. Vinatier was arrested immediately after the French president Macron said that France would send troops to Ukraine, in the worst Russia’s traditions of “hostage diplomacy”. About the same time 26-year-old native of Donbas with dual Russian and Ukrainian citizenship was detained in France on suspicion of preparing a terrorist attack. At the very first hearing on June 7 that sent him to jail on accusations of failing to register as a “foreign agent”, Vinatier was demonstratively thrown in a cage in the courtroom. At the hearing on July 4, the prosecution alleged that Vinatier was guilty of collecting military information. The prosecution didn’t disclose what information Vinatier shouldn’t be privy to, but stated that it "could be used against state security." The accusation of not registering as a “foreign agent” — which Vinatier said he wasn’t aware he was required to do — is usually reserved for Russian citizens who are financed by foreign entities and involved in political activities. But recent changes to the law require anyone who “collects information on military issues” to register as a “foreign agent”. The 48-year-old Frenchman is an adviser with the Geneva-based ‘Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue’, a Swiss conflict mediation organization, and a long-time researcher of Russia and other post-Soviet countries. Russia has been using its "foreign agent" laws to jail domestic critics for a long time, and now the regime is doing it to foreign citizens as well. On June 21, 2024, Vinatier was included in the Russian register of “foreign agents”. Vinatier attended the court hearing on July 4 via a video link from the detention centre — he wasn’t brought to the court. The judge extended his detention until August 5. Any foreign citizen in Russia is a potential hostage and an instrument of exerting pressure on democratically elected governments, especially during elections. Hostages are also used as leverage in negotiations. Kremlin bots are pushing such topics in social media to stir emotions and cause division. In case of Vinatier, Kremlin bots are already driving the story to notoriety. Under the current accusation, Vinatier can be imprisoned for up to 5 years.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Why does the current Russian military seem so incompetent?
Answer: The current Russian military doesn’t just seem incompetent — they are incompetent. And corrupt — from top to bottom. A Russian contract soldier who deserted and escaped to the West told about the disarray and corruption in the Russian army to Verstka Media. Anton (not his real name) decided to sign a contract with the Russian army to pay off the debts. Anton was struggling to repay loans amounting to 1 million ruble ($10,000). In Russia, most people don’t earn such money in a year. It were the bailiffs who convinced Anton to sign up for the war in Ukraine. Ads for army contract service are plastered all over Russia. (Stock photos are used throughout this post.) The conditions they offered sounded great: a contract with the civil organization JSC Investinform (it gets paid for recruiting soldiers for the war with Ukraine), plus the regional payout on sign up, plus payments from the Ministry of Defense. In total, Anton was supposed to be earning about 350,000 rub. per month ($3,500). In August 2023, Anton arrived in Moscow, signed a 1-year contract with the Ministry of Defense and an employment contract with JSC Investinform. The second contract allowed him to get top-up payments in addition to the standard 215,000 rub. ($2,150) MOD wage to Russian soldiers in Ukraine. That’s how Moscow officials meet the allocated quotas of soldiers per region: on paper, these recruits are Muscovites, but in reality, it’s deprived residents of small Russian towns living in poverty that are sent to the war. Muscovites have no desire to die for Putin; they live quite well. Think ‘Hunger Games’ districts and the Capitol: that’s Russia and Moscow. On sign up, Anton was immediately paid 400,000 rub. ($4,000). All debt collection proceedings against him had been suspended — that’s another “perk” offered to desperate Russians in need, to convince them to sign up for the war. However, he couldn’t use the money to repay the debts. Instead, he was forced to spend the money he got upfront to buy a proper uniform and personal protective equipment — bulletproof helmet, vest, etc. When new recruits arrived to the army training grounds, they were given some ancient uniforms and combat boots — all of them were 4–6 sizes too large. The helmet was from the times of WWII, a piece of shrapnel would pierce it like paper. But as soon as they arrived to barracks, helpful “intermediates” arrived, eager to sell to the fresh recruits all they needed. Nothing in the Russian army was for free. If you came to “earn big money”, you first needed to buy your own gear. The newbies had to pay the full retail price for their clothing and equipment. On top of that, they had to pay for parts for the machinery they would be using in the future. Some lame excuse was offered to make them pay for parts. Basically, commanders know how much cash you have been just paid, and extract it all before you have a chance to spend it. $4,000 went quick. The workers of the military warehouse where they were supposed to get equipment and uniforms were all drunk. Half of the officers were drunk as well. Quickly the recruits learned that they had to buy not only their own military gear but also food: within 2 weeks, all soldiers got food poisoning from eating the meals in the military canteen. So, they had to buy food in the local kiosk, where a liter of milk cost $8. The shop assistant was driving a luxury Mercedes, Anton says. Corruption in the Russian army is all-permeating. Because of Anton’s vocal complaints about the equipment, he was sent to a “Storm-Z” unit after the training course. Storm-Z is the “penal brigades”, where murderers and robbers recruited from prisons and deserters who were caught are shipped. Out of 600 recruits delivered to the front with him, only 40 survived after 2 months of assaults near Kupyansk. “It was just some kind of extermination. From one company, 5–6 people would return alive. The tanks and armored carriers were also smashed. In the end, we were mixed with prisoners and were simply pushed, pushed, pushed ahead.” How did he survive? “How I survived is a good question. I was a grenade launcher, not a stormtrooper, I didn’t go in attacks. We operated from hidden positions. Direct fire in these fields is not an option,” recalls Anton. “In 9 cases out of 10, storm troops are liquidated on approach.” “There are no experienced people in the infantry; people run away. If a person survives, he refuses to go on attacks, he starts having anxiety and hysterics. People rather go to jail than go on attacks.” In the village of Zaytsevo (Luhansk region), there is an unofficial jail where the Russians are holding soldiers who refused to continue to fight. Some of them say it’s “hell”, but it surely beats dying under heavy artillery fire trying to storm fortified Ukrainian positions. “The losses were simply insane, I lost count. For 3 kilometers, which were eventually taken back by the Ukrainians, 5–6 companies were killed,” According to Anton, the commanders are reprimanded for heavy losses, so all of those who haven’t returned from the attack are reported as “missing” (presumed deserters), not killed. Anton was deployed from the beginning of October till the end of November 2023. By that time, only a few people were left in his unit. They were taken in the rear of Russia-occupied Luhansk region, where they had to train the new recruits — prisoners and contractors. Then suddenly they were loaded on trucks and shipped to a camp in the Belgorod region (Russian territory near the border with Kharkiv region of Ukraine). By mid-March 2024, they were sent on the location near the Ukrainian border. Their unit was loaded on trucks (most Russian armed personnel carriers are destroyed by now, the troops are moved around by trucks) and for the whole night and the next day their column was driving on roads. Anton didn’t know that a raid by “Freedom of Russia Legion” was ongoing in the Belgorod region for already 3 days. He says that their commanders also didn’t know what was going on. Their trucks got under artillery fire. One of Anton’s colleagues was killed in a strike. His group hid at a cottage of a 90-year-old granny. No one knew what to do, commanders didn’t give any orders. They were under fire for several hours. Only the next morning the commanders contacted them and told them where to go. By that time, all locals escaped the village, stores and offices didn’t operate. The soldiers were ordered to stay in the local school, which was also closed. The soldiers simply hid there and slept. Communication with the base wasn’t working. They were under artillery fire, drones circling above the place. “We heard the conversations of our comrades, but we could not answer. There was an attack and breakthrough at their positions. Not only Storm-Z units were there but also border guards. In the meantime, it turned out that a whole platoon had been demolished in the woods.” Later the same day Anton went with a group to evacuate the wounded and dead from the battlefield — he had to replace the deceased colleague, although he hadn’t done evacuations before. During the evacuation, the group had to shed their weapons and armor, which weighed up to 50 kg, and walked 5 km back to the school. (The wounded guy that Anton evacuated died in the hospital.) In the basement, where the school canteen was, they took some sleep. As they woke up, they had to go back to get their weapons. Anton marked the location where he hid his grenade launcher on the map with an asterisk. “If I lost the grenade launcher, I would be transferred to the infantry, and infantry means certain death. Machine guns and rifles are dime a dozen, but it’s nearly impossible to procure something mightier.” Anton says that once his commander opened up and blurted: “I don’t give a f**k about you contractors, they’ll send me as many of you as I need — but for the lost equipment I would be hauled over the coals, it’s a lot of paperwork.” In storm troops, losses reach up to 90%, says Anton. He believes that if it weren’t for aerial bombing by the Russian Air Forces, the units of Russians that are fighting for Ukraine (“Freedom of Russia” Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps, who were responsible for the raid on the Russian territory) would have easily captured the border areas of the Belgorod region with the help of FPV drones and artillery. Ukraine is superior to Russia by half a century in technical terms, their artillery is more accurate, and drones constantly conduct reconnaissance, Anton says. After the raid, the commander of Anton’s unit went on a drinking binge — along with his entire headquarters. The commander blamed the signalman for the failure in communications and began beating him up — after a few days of the torture, the signalman deserted. Meanwhile, Anton himself was thinking about doing the same thing. At the end of March 2024, he was watching a video of Russian oppositional channel ‘TV Dozhd’ (they were banned in Russia in 2022 and now broadcast from Europe), which mentioned the organization that helped Russian soldiers to escape the army and desert from the front (‘Idite Lesom’). At first he was skeptical, but when rumors about an upcoming offensive in the Kharkiv region spread, decided to give it a go. Anton says he realized that it’s impossible to survive in the Russian storm troops. Before agreeing to sign the contract, he had completely different ideas what it would be like. He asked the commanders to take 3 days off, but they refused. He couldn’t get a leave either — he says that even mobilized soldiers who serve since September 2022 can’t get a vacation. But he managed to get commanders’ permission to leave the unit for 1 night — until the morning. “Almost everyone who has been behind the front line thinks about escaping,” says Anton. 1.5 months after his escape, he cannot adapt to the peaceful life in a safe European country. Sometimes he has panic attacks and adrenaline rushes, but he tries to suppress them. His attitude towards the war in Ukraine has changed greatly. “There is guilt on me,” admits Anton. ”Once, our detachment commander broke down, drunk: “Yes, we are f***ing orcs!” “It’s disillusionment. The commanders don’t show it, and such coming outs happen mainly because they are drunk. During my time there, my entire outlook on life changed. I no longer feel anything positive about the Russian state. This is not a war, but some kind of agony. The only parallels that emerge are with the World War 1. We are simply being sent to slaughter,” concludes Anton. He plans to stay in Europe and apply for political asylum. He believes that he has the right to claim it as “a person who refused to participate in war crimes.” He never fully repaid the loans — and has no plans to do it.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How do you recognize Kremelbots, paid Russian propagandists posting on social media?
Answer: Yesterday, all paid Russian propagandists posted fake news about the wife of Ukraine’s president, Olena Zelenska, buying a luxury Bugatti car for $4.5 million — and today Bugatti denounced the failed Russian disinformation campaign and filed a criminal complaint for forgery, use of forgeries, usurpation of identity and defamation. The known Russian shills who posted the fakes immediately after the “news” popped up on the fake “French media website” must be really concerned today. Bugatti has enough money to bankrupt them, and their lame excuses are unlikely to stand in the court of law. The fake news was reprinted by the mainstream Russian media, all of which quoted the mock-up French website ‘Vérité Сachée’, which never existed until 9 days ago. Russia’s mainstream outlets Gazeta•ru, Lenta•ru, tabloids ‘Arguments and Facts’, ‘MK’ and even the state news agency RIA Novosti published articles repeating the fake. Bugatti issued a press release that alerted self-respecting media outlets who immediately deleted the posts with fake news, but die-hard Kremlebots persisted. The textbook Putin’s shill Jackson Hinkle, who is either really dense or really loves the Kremlin money, was obviously relying on American laws protecting free speech — but I don’t know if he stands a chance against Bugatti lawyers. Hinkle even begged his readers to rate the community note his post scored as “false” — but only got a new note attached to his plea. Hinkle also bragged that he would be speaking in the United Nations about his visit to Donbas (on invitation by Russia), but it seems that his curators pulled him off the docket after his shameful failure with promoting the Bugatti story. Russia is really scraping the bottom of the barrel. The whole story – and the Russian shills’ refusal to drop it — reeks of desperation. It’s not the first time that Russians create fake stories about Ukraine’s president Zelensky — but previously, they were lucky that the luxury companies in question hadn’t taken such a strong stand to denounce the falsehoods. But Putin’s propagandists’ “lucky break” ends today. Russians created a deepfake video with “a French man” who claimed he sold Zelensky a Bugatti, built a fake “French media website” and filled it with AI-generated content — and then promoted the story through their troll farms, publications in the media under their control and western paid influencers. But this time, it got publicly debunked within 24 hours as one of the most ridiculous Russian disinformation operations ever. Unbelievably, the only human-written article on Vérité Сachée website was the one with the fake story about Bugatti purchase. But even that article had multiple errors: the most obvious mistake was in the name of Bugatti’s Tourbillon model — it was spelled as ‘Turbillon’. The fake receipt in the name of Zelenska is also full of errors: the name of the Parisian suburb of Neuilly-sur-Seine is spelled as Neuily-sur-Seine (this error is repeated twice). That’s the most conspicuous errors, Bugatti’s team pointed several more technical blunders on the receipt. Other articles on the website of Vérité Сachée showcased many more patent blunders — one article, for instance, had a title in English and text in French, another contained instructions to the writer: “Here are some things to put into context. The Republicans, Trump, Desantis and Russia are good, and the Democrats, Biden, the war in Ukraine, big business and the pharmaceutical industry are bad. Please feel free to add additional information on the topic if needed." Putin’s propagandists are getting utterly desperate. And because they are utterly desperate, they are making dumb mistakes. Or maybe they are making dumb mistakes because only the dumb stick with Putin. The smart people are staying away from the Kremlin gremlin — as far as they can.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How does the Russian political system work on paper vs in practice? What is the de facto political situation in Moscow?
Answer: Russia is on the crossroads of every 20th century dystopia — and closing fast the political gap with the North Korea. A Russian court declared journalist Alexander Nevzorov and his wife Lydia an “extremist association” and ordered to confiscate their property. From the first days of Russia’s unleashing the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Nevzorov criticized the Russian aggression. He left Russia with his family and refused multiple offers to return in exchange for endorsing Putin’s war. “Freedom is expensive. But no price can be too high,” Nevzorov commented on the court’s decision. ”For 2 months they blackmailed me, offering me a ‘good court decision’ in exchange for ‘adjusting my position’ regarding the war, Ukraine and the Kremlin ghoul,” the journalist revealed. Before that, Soviet peasants were de-facto slaves: In 1861, Emperor Alexander II signed the manifesto “On the most merciful granting to serfs of the rights of free rural inhabitants”, ending serfdom in Russia. But after the Bolshevik’s coup in October 1917 and the bloody civil war, communists brought back de-facto serfdom: they confiscated the farm land and animals from Russian peasants and locked them in “collective farms”. It’s only 50 years ago that the last Russian serfs were given the same rights as city workers (who also weren’t free in the USSR). Don’t believe the lies that marxists tell you about communism and socialism (in fact, when the Soviet communists failed to build communism for several decades, they simply named it “socialism” and told the masses that communism will follow soon). There had been no country in the history of the mankind that attempted to build a Marxist state and didn’t produce a totalitarian tyranny. Not even one.

Question: What is it like to live in Cuba?

It’s full of abuse, misery, hunger, violence and other numerous achievements of Marxism that some maximalists in Europe and America dream about. Many Cuban city streets look like a giant dumpster. (Video in the comments below). The recently built K23 hotel in Havana is towering over slumps, allowing to see all the destruction of the island from its heights. The level of despair in Cuba is such that Russia is recruiting mercenaries there. The influx of foreigners into the ranks of the Russian army increased after ‘Wagner’ was removed from the scene of the war in Ukraine, following Prigozhin’s mutiny in June 2023. Mercenaries from Cuba, Nepal, Sierra Leone, and Somalia who fought for Russia have been captured by the Ukrainian army. A captive from Cuba said that he agreed to fight in Ukraine because of the “big money” he was offered: 250,000 rubles per month (USD$2,500). It’s actually more than the Russian contractors get paid. Castro’s version of socialism has been imploding for decades. Cubans were led to believe that things would change and improve, but through decades of misery and repressions, Cubans had to settle for crumbs, waiting for a miracle. In 1980s, the propaganda insisted that all Cuban products were “the best in the world.” The USSR was the mighty empire that would back Cuba up, no matter what, and “it would be just a matter of time until the communism arrives”. When 1990s arrived, Cubans handed over their most precious relics, possessions and jewelry in exchange for a small check that allowed them to buy a color television or a fan with a light. Cubans handed in their treasures to be able to own a TV, which fed them more propaganda. In 1991, the USSR collapsed and the Soviets left Cuba. But another benefactor arrived in no time: China brought its Haier refrigerators, along with pots and pans — the only problem here, not much food to cook and refrigerate. The hope for a miracle rejuvenated, maybe the Chinese would help to fix Cuba’s economic disaster? When this didn’t eventuate either, Fidel Castro decided to allow private entrepreneurship, and people again had high hopes, began brainstorming ideas and business plans. Cubans began buying and selling stuff, investing, borrowing. Until the regime changed its mind and began taking away business licenses and banning whole sectors, like 3D cinemas, just like that. No apologies or compensations. Then Obama became the president of the USA, and Cubans again began hoping that things would get better — that the Americans would finally "invade" Cuba with their yachts, cars, and cruise ships, leaving bigs tips and showering locals with cash. These hopes crashed as well. Then Russia 2.0 arrived. And once again, Cubans were hoping that things would finally change, that this time they for sure would get out of poverty and misery. They were assured that this time there were real plans, projects and opportunities for everyone. Cubans forgot that the former USSR had been investing in Cuba 4 billion dollars per year, for 30 years. Nothing changed before, so why would things be different this time? Food shortages and energy blackouts are acute in Cuba. “No bread or milk, many kids don’t have breakfast, blackouts last 10+ hours per day.” The Castro regime stripped people of their dignity and made them dependent on its injustices. The worse they are treated by the regime, the more they defend it, because they need these crumbs. Socialism and communism are the cancer of the world.

Question: Is it true that wages in Russia are very low and the cost of living is very high?
Answer: A young Russian policewoman was fired for posting a reel on Instagram where she mocked her $400 (40,000 rub.) monthly salary, which is actually less than $100 per week. (Video in the comments below.) 28-year-old Olga Gaidukova worked as a district police officer in the town of Novocherkassk (Rostov region), population 160,000, which is in the South of Russia, near the Ukrainian border. The satiric reel about her salary, which she published in her personal Instagram account, scored a lot of views and likes. It is this popularity that got her in trouble. Reportedly, the young lady was called to her superiors, who demanded from her to delete the Instagram account — but she refused and was fired. The defiant ex-police officer admitted that she didn’t think her bosses would go that far. There aren’t too many willing candidates for such jobs and police officers are overworked. The cost of living keeps skyrocketing. Mortgage rates are at 17% in Russia, and the government just cancelled special rates for first home buyers (which were at 8%). “Prices are cheaper than they will be tomorrow!” — Russians bitterly joke about the constantly rising prices. The Russian central bank plans to raise the base rate, which is currently at 16%, so the mortgage rates could be going beyond the scary 17% per year already this month. Putin keeps saying that Russians can purchase more goods with their low salaries than westerners can buy with their much higher wages, but I don’t think many westerners would want to live on the ration of cabbage soup with bread and tea with cookies. This is actually what pensioners in Russia eat every day, because most of their pension money they spend on utilities bills (aka “kommunalka”). After paying for their homes, they can only spend $1–3 per day on food. And no, it’s not enough to buy proper food. Yes, Russian people working regular jobs live better than homeless people in America living in the streets. But they don’t live anywhere as comfortable as Americans who work in the same type of jobs. That’s a fact.

Question: Are there Russian citizens, currently living in Russia, that post anti-Russian government statements here and aren’t afraid of government reprisals?
Answer: 18-year-old Daria Kozyreva is one of the youngest political prisoners in Russia. 2 years ago she studied medicine in St. Petersburg State University. On February 24, 2024 — the 2-year anniversary of the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine — Kozyreva was arrested at the monument to Ukrainian poet Taras Shevchenko, for pasting a leaflet with his poem. She was charged with “repeatedly discrediting the Russian army” — the made-up offense for which she can be locked in prison for 5 years. Since her arrest, Kozyreva has been locked in a pre-trial jail in St. Petersburg, where she is awaiting trial. Because of repressions, most Russians are terrified to say anything against the war. At first, it was safe to simply stay silent, but by now Putin’s regime demands every citizen to support the war in Ukraine, following the mantra, “If you are not with us, you are against us.” From her prison cell, Daria Kozyreva wrote an open letter to Russians, calling them to speak up. It published by the Russian opposition publication ‘Holod Media’, whose editors were forced to emigrate from Russia. Open letter to Russian citizens “Russia is entangled in a heavy, impenetrable cocoon — a cocoon of silence. Just as any crime is committed with someone’s tacit consent, so any dictatorship is maintained thanks to the silence of the people. A colossus with feet of clay will be worth nothing if all those who disagree speak out. But they stay silent. Someone thinks that everything has been already decided and there is no point for him, a small person, to get involved in it. Someone hopes that others will say everything for him — only others also find excuses to remain silent. Meanwhile, the real reason for this silence is human fear, wild fear. No dictatorship can make everyone believe it — therefore it constantly resorts to fear, its first and last means of subjugating the people. The Germans in the era of Hitler obediently shouted “Heil”, realizing what could happen to them for disobedience; Soviet people during the Stalin’s era were afraid to whisper in their own kitchens for fear of being reported on. The steamroller of repressions does not even need to crush all those who disagree — just a few illustrative examples, and the rest will shut their mouths. The absurdity of Putin's repressions has reached such a degree that any little thing can become a reason for persecution — and no one knows exactly what to say anymore. The Kremlin villain is happy, that’s what the Kremlin villain needs. As long as everyone is silent, his own life will be safe. And that is precisely why you cannot remain silent. No, people’s fear is understandable: it is very difficult to risk their positions, their prospects, their freedom. In addition, many have families — such people are doubly scared. But will it be easier for these families to live under a dictatorship, under tightly tightened screws, behind the Iron Curtain? A dictatorship can continue to commit its atrocities, its lawlessness, as long as it feels strength and power. And nothing will change as long as everyone remains humbly silent. So, maybe it's time to speak up? Everyone who can speak must speak. The few who dared to speak are now too few for anything to move. Everyone who disagrees with the Moscow regime should speak out. It’s easy to send a few people to jail for their words — but only because there are so few of them. But there are not enough prisons in Russia for everyone, for all those who disagree. Even if the authorities build just as many new prisons especially for them. But when, having overcome fear, everyone starts talking, the time will come for Putin’s pack to be afraid. No evil lives forever, any dictatorship is sure to fall. It may fall under its own weight, as the USSR collapsed, or thanks to the people who finally rebelled. No doubt, when Putin’s dictatorship falls, there will be many people who will say they never supported the war or that they only formally supported it, to stay out of trouble. There will be even more people who will claim that they “had been deceived” and never knew real facts. Frankly, Putin himself constantly claims that he “had been deceived” by the West, by Ukraine, by “partners”. Russians choose to close their eyes and ears. They choose not to seek the truth, choose to follow the path that appears “safe.” That path is anything but safe, and the further down the line, the more precarious is to keep going along. No citizen of Russia who is currently living in Russia feels safe to post anti-Russian government statements here or anywhere online. They are all afraid of government reprisals — not only against them, but also against their families. They think they have too much to lose. They hope that things will work out somehow, without them having to do anything. They are so wrong. Because the worst is yet to come.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: When will Putin stop?
Answer: If Putin were locked in a prison cell, this madness of a full-scale war in Ukraine and constant Russian threats would certainly stop. Failing that (which would be only possible through an internal coup), Putin would be forced to stop if he could no longer draft enough soldiers to send to the war in Ukraine or was unable to equip them with weapons. Willingly, Putin might stop if he were given an appearance of a victory in Ukraine: something that he could announce to the Russian populace as a triumph. For 2.5 years of the full-scale war, the Russian populace had been diligently suppressed to the level where they don’t dare to speak up — they can’t even verbalize their dismay with being “best friends” with the North Korea, which for decades has been the butt of every joke about backward dictatorships. The Russian people have to swallow their nationalistic chauvinism and display satisfaction about “strategic alliance” of Putin and Kim Jong Un. Name: Elena Gold
Question: If Vladimir Putin learned he only had a few weeks to live, would he nuke the USA?

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Does Putin know he's going to lose?
Answer: Putin is convinced that he’s been appointed by higher forces to lead Russia to greatness, and he is confident that he simply cannot lose. The prediction by certain western analysts that if Donald Trump is elected, this would mean a win for the Russian army in Ukraine (which I personally do not share) keeps Putin’s hopes up that he only needs to last until this happens. And fifty million Germans believe in it with him,” wrote Erich Maria Remarque about Adolf Hitler. Timur Ivanov at the court hearing on June 20. Name: Elena Gold
Question: What does Putin wish to achieve?
Answer: Despondent Putin in North Korea, silently wishing to reset the world order to October 2021, to the version of history where he never attempted to bully NATO into submission. Frankly, I think that at this point, even Vladimir Putin himself doesn’t know what he wishes to achieve — except for the magic ability to time travel and change his own actions in the past. His plan to bully NATO spectacularly backfired — and Russians are paying a huge price for it, which will be echoing through decades and generations. For starters, in just months after Putin ordered his troops to bomb Ukraine, Russia became the most sanctioned country in the world, in response to inhumane atrocities it inflicted on Ukrainians. Nothing that Putin did before had produced such results: For over 2 decades, Putin was getting more and more imperious, and the response to the atrocities he caused to peoples of neighboring countries wasn’t strong enough to stop him venturing further. Putin’s attack on Ukraine could have been successful: if in February 2022, president Zelenskyy took the Americans’ offer to evacuate, as the 65-km-long column of Russian tanks was rolling towards the Ukrainian capital and Russian paratroopers were landing at the Hostomel air field 30 km from Kyiv, then it would be “game over” for Ukraine. Instead, Zelenskyy uttered the famous phrase: “I need ammunition, not a ride.” Putin hoped to cause an “anti-Maidan coup” in Ukraine. His plan was to re-install the expired president Victor Yanukovich, who escaped to Russia in February 2014, after months of unrest in Kyiv (initially caused by Yanukovich’s reneging on his pre-election promise that Ukraine would join the EU) — and after Yanukovich helped Putin (by not acting in Ukraine’s defence) to take over Crimea. Victor Yanukovich was the 4th president of Ukraine (25 February 2010 – 22 February 2014), who infamously escaped to Russia, where he now lives. After the re-reinstatement of Yanukovich (the application for reinstatement had already been quietly filed in a Kyiv court weeks before the February 2022 invasion, so it could be processed within a day, once Kyiv was under the Russian control), a new “election” would be called, in which Putin’s relative Medvedchuk would be “elected” as the new president of Ukraine. The plan was prepared in a great detail. Putin just didn’t foresee one thing: that the Russian troops wouldn’t be able to take Kyiv. And that Zelenskyy would be able to command the support of 95% of the Ukrainian population and lead the defence (in December 2021 — 2 months before the invasion — Zelenskyy’s approval rating in Ukraine was only 30%). Putin didn’t realize how strongly Ukrainians were united against becoming a part of Russia that when he nearly reached an agreement with the Ukrainian government in March 2022, under which Ukraine would “conditionally surrender”, he decided to add “the right of veto” for Russia on what happens to Ukraine if it’s being invaded again. The agreement that Ukraine nearly signed in March 2022 — weeks into the Russian invasion — is now all but an impossible dream for Putin. He keeps returning to its conditions and crying about the spilled milk, how the bloodbath that followed “could be prevented” — if Ukraine only agreed that Russia would be forever its ruler. The infamous “Istanbul March 2022 agreements” (which had never been fully agreed on by both parties or signed) included: And to these conditions, which the Ukrainian government was considering — Putin decided to add Russia’s “right of veto” on military aid to Ukraine in case if it ever was invaded. Basically, setting Russia to face no resistance in Ukraine when the Russian troops invade again. Russia is always doing this. This has been Russia’s modus operandi since they became a state in 1991. The old USSR still had some decency on the international stage; the Russian Federation, led by the KGB-trained clique, has none. It is content with acting in the most untrustworthy and barbaric ways. After February 2022, the masks are off — and so are the gloves. Putin’s Russia stopped hiding its inhumane essence and is gleefully demonstrating its brutishness. Putin hopes that this will save him from being ousted by his own people, whom he has promised the glory of superiority over Europe and America. Meanwhile, the reality is that he has to bow to China — and even North Korea — to be able to supply his troops, which otherwise would be exterminated in Ukraine. The huge, mighty Russia is unable to even hold onto 18% of the Ukrainian territory, without being propped by a little dictatorship of North Korea. But Putin’s wish remains to rule the world. He just needs to finally take in full the Donetsk region in Ukraine — which the Russians are trying to capture for 12.5 years — and for the West to agree that he’s the perfect person to decide who is allowed to do what, on the global scale. I don’t know how about the West, but Ukrainians are certainly not going to just give Putin what is not his.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Are people in Russia proud of the wonderful reception their much-loved leader Putin has received from another much-loved leader in North Korea? It must warm all Russian hearts to be able to witness such great love between two ideals and idols?
Answer: Kim gifted Putin a portrait of Putin that literally looks like a mirror that the evil king from ‘Shrek 1’ constantly consults. In the case of Putin, this is not far from the truth — he only takes his own advice. When the USSR dissolved in 1991, there were 1000’s of possible paths that Russia could take — and this is the one they took. In 24 years of Putin as the leader, Russians went from making fun of North Korea to ‘You are our last hope!’ “I can’t help but recall Colonel Putin’s previous visit to Pyongyang,” writes Russian photographer Artem Chernov. Chernov was there during Putin’s first visit to Pyongyang in July 2000, when the newly inaugurated Russian president went to meet Kim Jong Il, father of the current leader of North Korea. Chernov continues: “It seemed to us that we, civilized and advanced, had flown into the most outdated village in the world, into the clown world, into the ‘1937 sanctuary.” We laughed at every wild detail, we mocked the seriousness of the protocol, the decorated marshals who were thin as a rake, the gray jackets who did not let us leave the hotel, the civilians who were afraid to enter the elevator with us, our security guards who were terrified to be left alone with us (the Russians will recruit me!)... We looked down on them, with the sympathy of free people for the serfs... It seemed to us that we were so far ahead that these poor fellows could never catch up with us... We patted them on the shoulder... Now, with what is happening today, it simply looks like an impossible dream, an alternative reality. But it did take place 24 years ago, and I was there. And now this [North Korea] is our last ‘strategic partner.’ Greeting an elderly colonel with a waddle on the red carpet. A young and thriving outcast brother, a generous supplier of ammunition.” “No, please, you first...”Chernov bitterly ends his trip down the memory lane. It was bad enough when Putin had to be submissive to the leader of China — the country that lived in poverty in 1980s when most of these 70-year-old ministers were already successful Soviet apparatchiks. But now they have to bow to North Koreans, the most notorious world pariahs. In the negotiations room, where Russian ministers sat down, a North Korean staffer ordered them out: “No, our leader must enter first.” (Video in the comments below.) Desperate Putin keeps drugging his whole cabinet of ministers with him to foreign visits — first to China, now to North Korea. Expectation: Russia will rule the world. Reality: Russian ministers are kicked out of the room because the North Korean dictator “must enter first”. A memorandum of strategic partnership between Russia and North Korea has been signed. Finally, the world’s greatest superpower has found a worthy partner. Incredibly as it may seem, Russians see their leader buying drones from Iran, having tea with Taliban and making deals with the North Korea — and they still believe they are the good guys.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Having attacked another country, what do the Russians expect to get as a result?

That western leaders change and the next leader will cut off the aid to Ukraine (and Putin puts a lot of effort and money supporting these politicians online with an army of bots). How they were before February 2022. Follow me for more updates!

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How to recognize Russian propaganda? Please share useful tips with others.
Answer: The recent sudden increase in the Russian propaganda online is caused by Russia’s cyber troops using AI. And AI is vulnerable. Russia is massively increasing the number of messages that bots impersonating Americans and Europeans post in social networks, and the only reason why they are doing it is because they can’t win on the battlefield in Ukraine. Putin’s only hope is that the West stops supporting Ukraine. If the West continues to stand with Ukraine — and gives Ukraine more tools — this would mean the end of the Russian army in Ukraine.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Am I right in thinking the great Ukrainian Peace conference in Switzerland has turned out to be a massive flop and a waste of time?

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Why are many people saying that Vladimir Putin is winning the war?
Answer: Golf carts and motorcycles replaced armored personnel carriers and tanks in the Russian army. The only military technique that Russia has perfected is “meat waves”. Question: How many peoples in Baltic countries were killed because of the Soviet deportation?
Answer: On June 14, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia commemorate the day of victims of communist terror, mass Soviet deportations in 1941. Political prisoners were those who actively resisted the Soviet occupation. They were sent to concentration camps (GULAG). Often charges were made up and people were sent to GULAG just to make the numbers, as required by the NKVD plan on “ideological cleanup”. No one was safe. Many families were taken just to fill the quotas if the listed family couldn’t be found; others were taken because they had similar names to those listed. Some local collaborators just wanted to settle scores. Mass deportations provided the USSR with slave labour in underpopulated parts of its empire, but the main goal was to transform the Baltic countries from proudly independent, functioning states into permanently subservient provinces. 2 years earlier, in 1939, the Soviets and Nazis formed an alliance by agreeing in their Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact to illegally divide the European states between them through crimes of aggression, thus igniting the World War 2. The Baltic countries declared neutrality at the outbreak of WW2, but the Soviets used the pretext that they were supporting independent Poland against its Nazi-Soviet occupiers to execute the next phase of its planned aggression in the Baltics. In agreement with the Nazis, the Soviets invaded and occupied the Baltic countries, overthrew the governments, and staged their own fake elections to produce ‘winning’ candidates who would ‘request’ Soviet annexation. Obviously, this was all totally illegal under international and domestic laws of these countries. After liquidating politicians, the first wave of mass deportations in June 1941 aimed to decapitate the independent states. It targeted families of civil servants, military leaders, police officers, business leaders, intellectuals, and public figures. Before the deportations, there were mass shootings. Only those deemed “redeemable” (i.e. those who were innocent) were deported. Stalin’s ideology always was, “no person — no problem.” Living conditions in Siberia were extremely harsh, whichever group of deportees people belonged to. People were simply dropped off the train in the middle of nowhere, and had to build houses and find food by themselves. That is, if you even survived the journey. Many did not. Baltic people were always mostly agricultural nations, and had an extremely strong connection to their land, going back to the Baltic pagan religion, many elements of which are still part of the Baltic identity. Soviet deportations tore the very fabric of this identity. June 1941 deportations were conducted simultaneously across large parts of Eastern Europe, not only in Baltics. And deportations continued after the WW2. In total, over the years, the Soviets subjected an estimated 6 million people under their rule to forced migration. The Russification of occupied territories of Ukraine that we see today is an old Russian tradition, going back to the USSR and the Russian empire. Mass killings and deportation of people and bringing Russians to replace them is something Russia has never been made to answer for. In 2021 Putin ordered to close ‘Memorial’, the oldest human rights organization in Russia and a Nobel peace prize winner. Founded in late 1980s, its goal was to document political repressions in the Soviet Union and build a database of victims of the Great Terror and GULAG camps. Once again, Russians are supposed to forget the past and erase from memory all the crimes their ancestors participated in. Then, crimes against humanity and genocide can be committed without a single pang of conscience. We are seeing it now. Again. But just as Russian imperialism failed in the Baltics, despite (or because of) mass deportations, we know it will fail again against Ukraine.
