Question: Is Putin a threat to Eastern Europe?
Answer: Putin is a huge threat to Eastern Europe — that’s why Baltic and most Eastern European countries are the biggest supporters of Ukraine’s fight against the Russian invasion. If Putin’s plans were limited to Ukraine, he wouldn’t have tried to blackmail NATO, demanding the alliance to withdraw to pre-1997 borders in December 2021. The pompous ultimatum was made by Putin, so he could use it as a formal pretext to invade all other countries of the Eastern Europe and Baltics that became NATO members after the collapse of the USSR. Of course, Putin’s invasion of Ukraine has nothing to do with NATO. Ukraine wasn’t even close to becoming a member of NATO in February 2022, when Russian troops crossed the Ukrainian border. In 2.5 years of the war, Putin’s politicians and propagandists dropped most of these presences — they no longer are trying to claim that “they are liberating Ukrainians” or that they “don’t hit civilian targets”. Now, they are openly saying it’s all about annexing more land (claiming “it’s Russian historical lands”, “we are taking back what’s ours”). Any hits on civilian targets Putin’s propagandists announce “a strike on a NATO warehouse” or “the place where NATO soldiers were located”. They don’t care anymore that no one believes them. They are brazen in their arrogance: “And what will you do?” The claim “it’s our historic lands” goes well beyond Ukraine, with Putin stating that Russia is the USSR and the Russian empire, and repeating that “Russian interests must be respected”. It is only Ukraine's courageous resistance that gave Europe time to prepare for what Putin has planned for it. Already in spring 2022, Putin was planning to take over Moldova, immediately after the fall of Ukraine — which Putin was confident would be completed by the end of March 2022. Russia wages non-stop hybrid war against the NATO countries and is already escalating these activities into open acts of sabotage, endangering people’s lives. The sooner Putin is stopped and decisively beaten in Ukraine, the lower will be threat to the countries of the Eastern Europe — and the European Union as a whole.

Question: Here in the west we hear all kinds of things about Russia. What is it really like to live there? Is Putin liked and/or respected? Do Russians have a better life than they used to?
Answer: Putin’s propagandist for the youth, Yekaterina Mizulina, named her dog “Vova” (short for “Vladimir”, like Bob and Robert) — I suppose, as a reference to the Russian leader Vladimir Putin. 39-year-old Yekaterina “Katya” Mizulina posted a video on the enemy social network Instagram (banned in Russia) complaining that Vova wasn’t allowed on a flight in Russia — it was her first attempt to fly with a dog, and she failed to convince the airline staff to let him on. Obviously, Katya didn’t take care to do things right, hoping she’s a celebrity. Earlier this year, there were even rumors that Mizulina Junior (her mother is a senator) was a Putin’s lover. Obviously, Putin’s administration was just using Mizulina for his re-appointment show (aka “presidential elections”), flying her around on a state jet under the guard of FSO (officers of presidential security forces). Now, Katya is no longer on the list of privileged individuals and has to follow the rules for the regular people. For a long time, Putin was bragging that he sorted out “the terrible 1990s” and brought order to Russia. The 1990s were known as the time when many Russians struggled to survive (really didn’t have the money to purchase food) and violent crime skyrocketed. Remember, it was in 1989 that the USSR withdrew forces from Afghanistan, after the 10-year invasion. The soldiers who fought in Afghan came home and found themselves abandoned by the state, with no means to earn a decent living. As a result, many Afghan veterans joined the organized crime, where their skills to kill and intimidate were in demand. That’s what caused the wave of violent crime in Russia in 1990s. Putin pulled out tens of thousands of violent criminals, who had been sentenced to long prison terms, and sent them to Ukraine. In about 6 months, ‘Wagner’ recruited about 50,000 prisoners for the war in Ukraine. Since January 2023 — for already 1.5 years, it is the Russian ministry of defence that recruits criminals from prisons and jails — anyone accused of crime is now first of all offered to go to war, detectives don’t even try to build a case for the court, just offer an army contract. If the MoD is as productive as ‘Wagner’ was, that’s another 150,000 criminals who were given guns and trained to kill. By the way, the rate of reoffending in Russia’s penitentiary system is over 90% — 9 out of 10 criminals who served their prison terms, re-offend and end up in prison again. The criminals who were recruited by Wagner and managed not to die (as many as 30,000 of them) returned to Russia. The number of crimes, including rapes and murders (including violent offenses against children), has already risen sharply in Russia. The country is returning to the same “horrible times” as in 1990s that Putin’s propaganda used as an example of the absolute desperation, to promote advantages of the “order in the country” brought by Putin after his election in 2000. 1992: Street markets in Russia. The improvements in the level of life for people are deteriorating even faster. Once again, many people in Russia have no money to buy food — first of all, pensioners, who spend most of their pensions to pay for utilities and rates. The pensioners are now often seen digging in the rubbish bins near food stores, where expired produce is thrown in. Those who struggle but are too proud to dig in the rubbish bins, are trying to supplement their income by trading produce from their gardens or re-selling some junk. That’s what illegal street markets look now, under Putin’s rule: They don’t have permits to sell (these permits are expensive) and if there is a police raid, they get hit with hefty fines. (Or have to pay bribes to the police.) “1990s are back,” say the people who went through the hard times 30 years ago. And it’s not going to get better. It’s going to get worse.

Question: Do you think it is fair to call a westerner who supports Putin’s invasion and actively spreads Putinist propaganda in comment sections, a quisling?
Answer: Well, Moldova aren’t just calling the citizens who spread Putin’s propaganda a “quisling” (“traitor”) — they are amending the criminal code to prosecute spreading disinformation in the interests of other states as treason. The term “quisling” arose because in World War II, Vidkun Quisling, a Norwegian politician, volunteered to help the occupying Nazis rule Norway for Germany. Now the term is used to mean a traitor, especially one who collaborates with an enemy occupying force for personal gain. Quisling was arrested and tried for war crimes in 1945, and sentenced to death. He was executed on October 24, 1945. The parliamentary majority (PAS party of Moldova President Maia Sandu) proposed to expand the legal definition treason by adding another type of activity: “assisting a foreign state, foreign organization, anti-constitutional entity or their representatives to carry out hostile activities against the security of the state”. This would include, in particular, “carrying out disinformation campaigns, organized activities aimed at achieving hostile goals through disinformation, which may harm the sovereignty, independence, unity, indivisibility, security or defense capacity of the Republic of Moldova.” Russia is de-facto occupying 17% of the territory of Moldova — the areas called Transnistria and Gagauzia, since 1990s. Russia claims that Moldova violates the rights of the Russian population of these self-proclaimed “republics” (you probably never knew about their existence until today). Sounds familiar?

Question: Is it true that Vladimir Putin brought a Labrador to a meeting with Angela Merkel because she's afraid of dogs?
Answer: In January 2007, during the meeting with Angela Merkel in Sochi, Putin brought in his Labrador in front of the German Chancellor, who has a phobia of dogs. The episode attracted so much bad publicity that Putin began explaining himself to foreign media, starting 2016. His version is that “he didn’t know” and “everybody in the office loved the dog” that had been, according to Putin’s version, always casually walking around the residence. Since then, the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti re-published the story explaining that Putin “didn’t do it to cause harm” several times — on February 20, 2022, for instance, 4 days before Russia invaded Ukraine. Merkel refuted Putin’s explanation that “he didn’t know” about her phobia of dogs. Merkel visited Moscow, Russia, after being elected chancellor in 2005, where she met with Putin, and he told her that he knew about her “dog problem” — and presented her with a big plush toy of a dog. “Even then, Putin told me that he had heard about my problems with dogs, and gave me this huge stuffed dog,” recalls Merkel. It was during that meeting in Sochi in 2007 that Putin told Merkel for the first time that he considered the collapse of the USSR to be the most terrible event of the 20th century. And she replied that for her it was a happy moment in her life, which allowed her to freely control her destiny.

The opposition wants to make their point that intimidation and threats won’t work. Earlier this month, the parliament approved the law on “foreign influence”, which the opposition calls, “the Russian law.” It’s feared the law will be used by the ruling party to persecute the opposition and position itself to hold power onto the power in Georgia, facilitating its leaning towards Russia, instead of the European Union. 85% of Georgians want the country to join the EU. President of Georgia Salome Zurabishvili vetoed the law, but the ruling ‘Georgian Dream’ party has enough votes in parliament to override the veto. ‘Georgian Dream’ plans to reconsider the law in the parliament next week. The mass protests of Georgian citizens weren’t effective in convincing members of ‘The Georgian Dream’ party to vote against the law, but maybe the incentives of the EU and the USA will offer a useful perspective.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What are the chances of a coup against Putin?
Answer: Putin has never been that close to a coup against him in the last 6 months. Since successfully dealing with ‘Wagner’ mutiny in June 2023 and liquidating its leader Prigozhin in August 2023, Putin’s position seemed to have strengthened. So much so that Putin was feeling confident in liquidating jailed opposition leader Alexei Navalny a month before his re-appointment show, scheduled for March 2024. And then Putin painted the incredible 87% public support for himself at “the presidential election”, which also went smoothly. Seemed like Putin could do anything and nothing could shake his throne in Russia. Until he decided to stage a decapitation strike on his ministry of defence — in the middle of the actual war that Russia fights in Ukraine. It means, the generals are commanding hundreds of thousands of troops that have loaded weapons in their hands. The real reason behind Putin’s sudden 2-day visit to Belarus is now becoming more obvious — Putin is simply terrified of a coup against him. That’s why he suddenly flew to Belarus on May 23, arriving at 11 pm at nigh. Apparently, Putin’s sudden escape to Belarus had something to do with him fearing the rest of Russian generals might not be so willing to patiently wait for an FSB team to transport them to a cell in Lefortovo. His newly appointed defence minister Andrei Belousov arrived the next morning by a military plane, landing at a military air field near Minsk. If Putin was safe and sound in his position in Russia, wouldn’t he and Belousov arrive together? Meanwhile in Russia, arrests in the ministry of Defence and among the General Staff are in full swing — as are “resignations” and dismissals. Obviously, the information that Putin is getting from the FSB shows that chances of a coup against him are quite high.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Are the recent arrests of top Russian military officials an indication of Putin reasserting control over the Defence Ministry?
Answer: Putin isn’t just trying to reassert control over the Defence Ministry by purging the top Russian military officials — he’s trying to change the existential paradigm of the Russian state. There is a lot of discontent among the so called Russian “elites”, who were allowed to steal from the state for 25 years of Putin’s governing. The deal was to be loyal to Putin, in exchange to the opportunity to enrich themselves through government contracts: businessmen were buying cars and real estate for state officials, giving them cash bribes, to get lucrative government contracts. The officials also had to “share” — pay up a share of what they stole, to their superiors. Rumor has it, the bribe to get the position of a general in the ministry of defence was USD 1 million, and then you were supposed to get your money back by getting kickbacks on allocating government contracts. The latest victim of Putin’s purge: Vadim Shamarin, deputy chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces. Now, the FSB — definitely on Putin’s approval — began arresting generals and top defence execs precisely for acting in their normal manner. Moreover, the episodes the generals are arrested for are from several years ago — as far as 2016. The FSB was aware of these “crimes” for years. And there are certainly much more in the FSB files — every Russian government official has a file in the FSB with his or her “sins” carefully documented. General Ivan Popov, former commander of the 58th army, was also arrested for corruption. The chief of General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, was reportedly livid about the arrests of his people. There was an announcement that the investigative committee asked to allow Popov to be detained under house arrest, but this request was withdrawn by prosecution just before the court — Popov will remain locked in prison. Lt Gen Yuriy Kuznetsov remains jailed in the infamous Lefortovo prison in Moscow pending trial. What is happening in the Russian ministry of defence is much bigger than just Putin’s trying to reassert his control. It’s a massive ideological shift. Putin plans to replace the team of old generals, who are used to stealing heaps with a new team, who (ideally) will be laboring for the idea — or, at the very least, steal very moderately. Arrested generals: Shamarin, Popov, Ivanov, Kuznetsov. Problem is, all the officers in the Russian army learn to steal, starting from the very bottom level of junior lieutenant. Their wages are so small in the time of peace, they struggle to survive otherwise. They are all thieves. So, they identify with the arrested thieving generals much more than with hypocrites pretending that they are clean (no one in Putin’s ranks is). And these colonels who hoped to become generals one day, they all were dreaming of the high life and privileges — not about living modestly and working 16 hours a day to please the Tsar. For 25 years, the system was training its elements that money and perks were the reward for smothering your conscience. Will Putin find enough unmercenary hopefuls, who believe in his vision of great Russia? Not very likely — everyone in Putin’s system is the product of the system. And let’s not forget that Putin is trying to rebuild the system in the middle of the war. Even Stalin realized that arresting generals during the war would be insane. During the war, Stalin released all the generals who were arrested during the purges of 1937–1938 and weren’t executed, reinstalled them in the same rank and had them lead the troops into the battle. Putin began the purge during the war — in fact, he conducted his own decapitation strike on the MoD and Army. Obviously, it was Putin’s plan to purge the army all along!

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What is the current border situation between Estonia and Russia?
Answer: Last night, Russia removed the light buoys delineating the border between Russia and Estonia in the Narva river. This happened after previous reports that Russia intends to unilaterally change its maritime borders with Finland and Estonia. As Putin’s plan to “encircle Kharkiv in 2 days” miserably failed in the East of Ukraine, Russia is staging provocations right, left and centre. According to Eerik Purgel, head of the Border Guard Bureau of the Ida-Viru County, Estonia and Russia install buoys on the Narva River to mark shipping routes every spring. The buoys need to be repositioned because the riverbed changes over time, so the fairway markings are reviewed each spring. Prior to Russia's full-scale invasion into Ukraine, the buoys were installed largely by mutual agreement. However, starting in 2023, Russia has not agreed with Estonia’s position regarding the placement of buoys. This year, Russia said it disagreed with the location of about half of the planned 250 floating markers. Estonia has installed light buoys in Estonian waters based on the State Border Act and the locations of the buoys that were mutually agreed between border agencies in 2022. "We decided to install floating signs for the summer season in accordance with the agreement of 2022 because they are needed to avoid navigation errors so that our fishermen and vacationers do not accidentally enter Russian waters," Purgel explained. Estonian Prime Minister Kaja Kallas stated at the weekly press conference that this is a border incident and the exact circumstances are being clarified. Margus Tsahkna and Kaja Kallas. Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna emphasized that the incident must be approached in a calm manner, as Russia is behaving provocatively. The incident fits the pattern of Russia's behavior in recent years, Tsahkna said — other border incidents have occurred, such as airspace violations. And it’s not only Estonia that’s targeted by Russia: similar incidents occurred on Russia’s borders with Lithuania and Finland as well. As the date of the World Peace Summit in Switzerland is getting closer (the Peace Summit is scheduled for June 15–16, 2024), we can expect more provocations from Russia. They just can’t help themselves.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What will be the effects of all the purges Putin is doing to the Russian Army?
Answer: Putin’s purge of the Russian army generals continues: The commander of the 20th Army Sukhrab Akhmedov has been removed from his post. Also yesterday, the head of the Department of Defense Procurement, Vladimir Verteletsky, was arrested and accused of bribery. Verteletsky is accused of taking a bribe “of an especially large scale”: allegedly, he received a car and a house from an entrepreneur working with state defense orders. The house was registered in the name of Verteletsky’s family member. His arrest continues the string of scandalous detainments of top military generals and executives of Russia’s ministry of defence. 4 previously arrested generals and ministry of defence execs: army generals Popov and Shamarin, Shoigu’s deputies Ivanov and Kuznetsov. A source in the Lefortovo prison in Moscow, controlled by the FSB, tipped that a special section was being prepared for impending mass arrests of army generals. The cells are being equipped with high-tech listening devices to pick up even the quietest of whispers. By the looks of it, paranoid Putin is trying to avoid another military coup, similar to the one of Yevgeny Prigozhin’s in June 2023. There is a lot of dissent among the ranks of the military, and at some time or another, probably all generals cursed their superiors and Putin himself. Such criticism of Putin used to be the norm in private conversations between army generals, but that was last year. Now any dissent can land you behind the bars. Seems like Putin is planning something so heinous, he wants to make sure that the chain of command is unbreakable — that no one will say, “No, I’m not doing it.” A lot of army generals are probably now wishing they supported Prigozhin a year ago, and not just stood aside.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How have Ukrainian forces demonstrated their ability to cause chaos far from the front lines?
Answer: As Putin was landing in Belarus last night — for a surprise meeting with Lukashenko, a massive aerial attack on military targets in Crimea shuttered the Russian-occupied peninsula. (Video in the comments below.) The Ukrainian Armed Forces attacked Crimea using drones and ATACMS missiles. Explosions were heard in Yalta, Alushta, Dzhankoy, Simferopol, Yevpatoriya and Bakhchisarai. Reported Ukrainian strikes on Crimea last night. Apparently, the locations of 126th Russian coastal defense brigade got hit, as well as the FSB military unit near Alushta. A military communications unit was hit near the village of Semidvorye. At least 6 MGM-140 ATACMS ballistic missiles hit the communications center of the radar and air defense forces of the Russian Army. Locals report that 4 ambulances and 2 fire trucks rushed along the highway at high speed towards the village in Simferopol district. The explosions were so big that nearby buildings were shaking. Meanwhile in Russia, the head of Rosneft demanded money from the state to protect oil refineries from drones. Igor Sechin wrote a letter to prime minister Mikhail Mishustin after Rosneft was forced to shut down 4 large oil refineries. Mikhail Mishustin, Igor Sechin. Reportedly, Russia already lost 20% of its fuel production, creating serious logistics problem not only for the Russian military, but also for the agriculture industry, which requires a lot of fuel during the summer season. At the same time, the annexed regions of Donbas will be soon separated from “the old Russia” by a border strip, like in the old days the USSR had large open fields on the border. Putin doesn’t really seem to believe that “Donbas will stay in Russia forever”, as Russian propagandists insisted. Actions speak louder than words.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What do you think will happen during Putin's talks with his Belarusian counterpart Alexander Lukashenko?
Answer: Last night, closer to midnight, Putin landed in Belarus. Officially, for a 2-day visit to discuss important state matters. In reality, Putin’s most pressing motivation to get out of Russia is probably to hide from problems arising from his mass arrests of top generals from the Ministry of Defence and General Staff. Lukashenko met Putin at the airport. (Video in the comments below.) The 2 dictators hugged. Putin said that he planned to discuss with Lukashenko “security issues and the second phase of Russian nuclear exercises with the participation of the Belarusian military.” But that’s just the PR, to mislead the public — KGB trained Putin to never tell the truth and always create the smokescreens. Being in Russia as top generals are getting arrested, that’s too much for sensitive Putin’s nerves, and that’s why he asked his mate Lukashenko to host him for a couple of days. The Kremlin news angencies emphasize that “Putin arrived on invitation of Belarus president”. If anything, Lukashenko doesn’t need much from Putin, except to be left alone — and money, of course. The miserable failure of Putin’s “Kharkiv in 2 days” operation that Shoigu prematurely launched on May 10 (it was planned for May 15–16), hoping to avoid being fired (didn’t help), as well as successes of the Ukrainian armed forces in destroying the Russian air defense and communications in the occupied Donbas and Crimea, using combined drone and missile attacks, made Putin’s position in Russia even more prone to being ousted by a military coup. Since he’s anyway there, Putin probably will try again to pressure Lukashenko to send Belarus troops to Ukraine, which he had been trying for over 2 years. Lukashenko will again find reasons to refuse to do it. Lukashenko may agree to stage a few provocations against Poland and Lithuania on the borders, sending more migrants to cause trouble — he has been doing it for years, causing Poland to cordon off the border with Belarus. Lukashenko might also agree to allow some Russian troops to enter Ukraine from the territory of Belarus, thus stretching the Ukrainian defence. Again, this happened before, at the start of the invasion in February 2022 — although since then, Lukashenko didn’t let Russia to use the territory of Belarus to launch ground attacks on Ukraine. It’s less likely to happen, but who knows, what tempting offer Putin prepared for Lukashenko in exchange. One thing for sure, because the Russian media and Kremlin bots online are pumping the “nuclear threat” topic, this is exactly what this meeting is not about.
